utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today is Wednesday. Let me first greet you, Witness, and I'll greet the accused, the Defence counsel, Ms. West, and Mr. Scott, and the rest of their team, and my greetings to all the people assisting us. The Praljak Defence has the floor for their questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, we should like to ask that you allow General Praljak to cross-examine this witness, since we're dealing with questions that are limited to the various locations around Mostar and in Mostar, and the witness mentioned some of them, like Bijelo Polje and others. And as you know, Praljak is from the region, so he knows all those places very well, and in that sense has special knowledge of the subject. So it will be far easier for the two of them to communicate. Just to inform you, we have 15 minutes, roughly, plus 5 minutes from the Prlic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good morning to you, too, Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm going to show you some photographs first and some videotapes. But before I do that, would you answer this question: In the northern districts of Mostar, Vrapcici, and Bijelo Polje, from the time that the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, 1995, to the present day, has any -- have any important buildings been built, or roads, or factories, or dams, or high-rise buildings? So during all that time, has anything essentially changed in the area?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: General, sir, after the war in 1996 and from that time onwards, along the M-17 road a bridge has been rebuilt which was destroyed across the Bijela River. That's all. No other roads have been reconstructed. And as for the various buildings, only a market-place has been built, three or four supermarkets or market-places.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, we haven't seen one another for quite some time, and I'm sure, if the Judges would allow us, we'd have a friendly chat. But over the next 20 minutes, I should like to ask you to just answer my questions, because we're not really interested in market-places and the like. Now, the Bijela Bridge, we saw this mentioned in yesterday's document and saw that the BH Army had taken control of the bridge in April 1993. Now, to the best of your knowledge, up until the end of the conflict and the Washington Accords, did it ever lose control of the bridge? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And do you know that one section of the bridge could be used until October 1993, when we won't say who and how the other half of the bridge was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: One lane was in order; the other wasn't. Now look at 3D -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May we have 3D03789 put up on our screens, please. 3D03789 is the number, and 3D43-1385, which is the last of the three photographs I've provided. And I didn't manage to go through these photographs with the previous witness because of lack of time. So it's not this one; it's the next one. This is 789, that's right, but may I have 1385 as the next photograph, and those are the last digits. 3D03789, and the number of the photograph itself is 3D43-1385. What can I do now? 3D43-1385. Here it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is that something that we call the Bijela Bridge over there, Witness?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you tell me, on the assumption that the bridge was destroyed, on the assumption, I say, this road going the round-about route, and it was constructed when the bridge was constructed, is it open to traffic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you mark the bridge and the road? You can put a "1" by the bridge and a "2" for the road running down this bay, around this bay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We have a little problem with the SMART board, so if there's a hard copy that you have in your possession, we can use that. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I had hoped, at the beginning of this trial, that we would have large maps to put up on an easel for this trial, but there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If the Usher would be so kind to take the map from Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And just take a look at where the road to the left leads, and was that open to cars? It wasn't an asphalt road, but could cars pass that way?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: So number 1 for the Bijela Bridge, please; number 2 for the road going around the bay; and number 3, the other road to the left in the direction of the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness can draw around the road using his felt-tip pen, so we can see it properly. That's right. And then place a number there, please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, where does that road lead to, towards Jasenjani or where?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: To Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Glogova, that's correct. Now place your signature and the date on that map.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, might I request that you take into account the fact that we're now dealing with maps and it's a rather lengthy process, so as far as my time goes, perhaps you could be indulgent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Page 3 of document 3D03789, as marked by the witness, shall be given Exhibit IC01148. Thank you, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Next I'd like 3D03791 pulled up, please. 3D03791, the first of those maps. 001 are the last digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, what do we see here, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: A panorama of the northern access to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Next map, please, 002.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you mark "Vrapcici" and "Bijelo Polje" with arrows, number 1 for Vrapcici and 2 for Bijelo Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General. May I remind you again that we have a problem with the SMART Board. So if you have a hard copy, we can place it on the ELMO and we can mark it. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Bozo, have you got a copy of that picture?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give my copy to the witness, and that can be put on the ELMO. It has to be put on the ELMO. There's a technical problem, you see. No? Oh, it's okay now. Fine. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you now mark Vrapcici with an arrow, and another one for Bijelo Polje? So number 1, Vrapcici; number 2, Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you can't see the whole of Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you. Now indicate Bradina [as interpreted] Hill.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And place a "3" there.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we need just your signature there.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An IC number, Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 3D44-0002, as marked by the witness, shall be given Exhibit IC01149. Thank you, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Next map, please. The same number, but now it's 003. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, my question is as follows: Behind Gradina Hill, yeah, Gradina Hill, towards Streliste, you can see that on this map, was there a road that was open, and does it still exist today; and if so, would you mark it on the map, please, and put a number 1 by it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: It existed before, it exists today, and it's open to all types of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just mark it so we can see it.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And your signature.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An IC number, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honour Judge Antonetti.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you show us where the road emerges on the other side of that hill there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: It goes upwards, where we conducted training sessions during the targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And towards Vrapcici?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: You can't see that on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Never mind. Just show us the general direction.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Just draw the arrow down towards Vrapcici, behind the hill where the road descends.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's right. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And may I have an IC number for these maps, now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 3D44-0003, as marked by the witness, shall be given Exhibit IC01150. Thank you, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that during the war, protected from any possible HVO positions, both civilians and members of the BH Army could pass through that way?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Now may we have the next map, which is 0005. Yes, that's the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What do you see on that image, Witness? Do you see Hum Hill, for example?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Put a number 1 by Hum Hill.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question to you is this: The BH Army positions on the left bank of the Neretva River, and the HVO positions on the right bank, are they mirror images; that is to say, do the two sides see the same thing? What the BH Army sees is what the HVO sees? You have hills on one side and hills on the other side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, you were in Mostar. After the two sides separated in Mostar, could you, from any of the HVO positions, see the Neretva banks controlled by the BH Army from any point?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Do you mean Mostar or the broader region around Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Only that part of Mostar that was under the supervision and control of the BH Army, not what we can see from Hum Hill to the left and right.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: You couldn't see the Neretva River or the embankment from any point at all, from the buildings or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. So put your signature to that photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And may I have an IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. A copy of 3D44-0005, as marked by the witness, shall be given Exhibit IC01151. Thank you, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now under the same number, 3D -- it's still 3D, and it's 03791, that's the general number, and the picture itself is 0011. Mr. Peric, use a number 1 to mark what you see as the electric plant here.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And tell us which one that is.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: That is the hydroelectric power-plant of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark the road to Sarajevo, please, the main road, number 2.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: If the Neretva River flow -- runs south, which direction would that be? The left-hand side of the plant, after the clashes with the BH Army, whose possession was it in throughout the clashes?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks] it was under the HVO, as far as the dam. It was throughout the clashes, as far as the dam to the north. The houses you can see over there were BH Army-held. The village is called Rastani.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Move along the Neretva and then the left-hand side of the river, what about that side? Was that BH Army-controlled?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to know. No, the other side. That was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And then on the other side, who controlled that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Everything that we can see to the right of the road and all that, after the clashes on the 30th of June, who controlled that area?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: The BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now 0012. Please sign the map.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 3D44-0011, as marked by the witness, shall be given Exhibit IC01152. Thank you, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] 0012, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, what about the front part of this image that we see; isn't that the access road to Vrapcici, which begins when Bradina [as interpreted] stops?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now, point out the road that is not the M-17, which goes behind Gradina Hill. And then you see that stone over there? The colour photographs are much better than the black-and-white ones. I'm not sure why we don't have colour photographs. Can you mark that with a number 1, please?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And then the other road that you see over there, north of the houses here -- no, no, no, here. You have a look at the map, and look at the road. Oh, right, we have a colour photograph now. It's perfect. Look at your screen. There's a better view there. The screen.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Mark it, please, the road that you saw.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fantastic. Number 1 for the first road, number 2 for the other. Your signature, please, and an IC number.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IC number, please, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 3D44-0012, as marked by the witness, shall be given Exhibit IC01153. Thank you, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] 0018, please, our next map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's a photograph facing north, the access road to Bijelo Polje. My question: Parallel or not to the main road to Sarajevo, M-17, are there not many roads such as this one? Is it not possible to reach each single house in Vrapcici and Bijelo Polje by car?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Indeed, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sign the map, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks] THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And could I have an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Actually, there's no reason to sign this map, because it has not been marked in any way. There's no damage. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Put a number 1 on the road, then, and tell us roughly where this road is headed to.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks] Kuti Livac, north of Mostar, and then on to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear anything that the witness said because the accused is chafing with his documents against the microphone, the microphone creating too much noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It goes north of Mostar and ends up right on the way out of the Bijelo Polje depression, just outside Prenj and Salahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we have an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 3D44-0018, as marked by the witness, shall be given Exhibit IC01154. Thank you, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I'll be showing a video-clip from Google now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the number because the witness coughed. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] 3D03793. Could that be played, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is this the power-plant in Mostar that you indicated in the other photograph, Mr. Peric?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Where exactly is Vrapcici?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: To the right, in the same direction that the image is moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Put a number 1 there. Oh, I see, you can't put a number 1 there. All right, let's move on, then. How many parallel roads are there? Many - right? - next to M-17.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite many of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, please. We are now in Potoci. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Move on, please. Move on, please. Was that the end? Now the other one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now the continuation, sir. The Bijela Bridge, if you can see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please indicate the roads that one can take in the area, and tell us where they take you to.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: How am I going to show that on this Google imaging device? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] All right, all right. He'll describe everything in the end. Just let the map glide on. What can I do about this? Yes, yes, everything can be seen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you see the road to Glogova on this map?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it an asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can cars take that road as well?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move on. Does this move on to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Look at the road to the left. Is that an asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Any cars there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] That's as much as I have on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just interject a question. Witness, have you, yourself, driven a car over any of these roads or all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have taken most of these roads. But when I look at the photograph that I have here, the northern-most section is one that I've never taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And yet you say that it is negotiable with cars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about what the general asked. Is it negotiable? I said, Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And what kind of cars; any car, lorries, big trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All-terrain vehicles, jeep vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That means, negatively, not a normal car with two-wheel drive, and even less a normal truck or lorry for transportation of goods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trucks, but not the really heavy ones. The ones that you, in Europe, consider as trucks, those couldn't. The TAM trucks, smaller trucks, the small-cargo vehicles, yes, but the long-distance trucks could not take that road. A tractor with a trailer could take that road as well. A small Mercedes, a really nice, expensive one, could never take that road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But they would have to be four-wheel drive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I was trying to say, all-terrain vehicles or TAM trucks, the kind used for cargo under three and a half tons; tractors with a trailer, also, up to three or four tons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the transcript, to be perfectly safe, the other video that we last saw was 3D03794, which is the section between Bijela -- the Bijela Bridge and Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please listen carefully to my question. This is an important question, and I want to be sure that you understand the question. And I will listen to your answer carefully. It seems that the M-17 was sometimes under the fire of the HVO in Rastani. At least that's what we've been told. This being the case, could you tell us whether a Muslim civilian who would want to leave East Mostar by foot, be it a child, a woman, a man, or BH Army soldier -- so I would like to know whether this person could take the pass that we have seen on this Google imaging device, so could it take these paths that we've seen from Jablanica -- going to Jablanica --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- without being hit by HVO fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was certainly possible for no one to be harmed by infantry weapons. As for artillery, no one was entirely safe from artillery weapons in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As for the infantry, weapons that the HVO was using, it was impossible to see those people from there; therefore, they couldn't be targeted. The road between Mostar and Jablanica was a safe one for them. It wasn't a very comfortable road, like it is today, but it was safe, and one could take it with no trouble at all and still get there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question on this topic. Could you tell us whether a civilian or a BH Army soldier could leave East Mostar to go to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the BH Army control, they could have. I'm not sure if they actually took advantage of that, but the possibility was there. Each of the civilians who wanted to leave were free to leave. I'm not sure if their own military authorities allowed them to, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak, you have used up 28 minutes. You must finish, because Ms. West has two hours, there might be some redirect, and we're running short of time. I'm only putting essential questions to this witness. Otherwise, I just refrain from putting questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it would be fair to at least grant a total of three minutes because of the technical difficulty experienced during the examination. It wasn't our fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have three minutes, so use them wisely. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: First question: Who controlled the access to Dreznica right across from the Bijelo Bridge, the HVO Army or -- the HVO or the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: The BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Secondly, you said a Mercedes couldn't negotiate that road. What about a tractor? What about a cargo truck up to four tons or, for example, a Renault 4?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I've listed all of those, and the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thirdly, would it not be an obligation for the army to maintain a road that was important for them?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: It goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My last question: You were asked yesterday by Mr. Stojic's counsel: Did the Serbs target Mostar and the general area? And you said, As they saw fit, or, As they liked. Sometimes they liked us better and sometimes the other side, something to that effect. Sir, throughout the war, as far as you know, did the Serbs target the left-hand riverbank and the right-hand riverbank of the Neretva River and the general Mostar area whenever they liked? Yes, there's some sort of music playing. I'm not sure what it is. I have no idea what that is. Were the Serbs, in fact, not firing whenever they liked, and, sure enough, they weren't short of ammunition, were they?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: What about after the clashes between the HVO and the BH Army? Did they not continue to, A, aid the BH Army and, B, target BH positions in and around Mostar all at the same time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Mr. Peric, I have no further questions. I thank you for coming here and answering these questions. Your Honours, I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just set the record straight, General Praljak asked a question: Under whose control was the territory near the Bijela Bridge? The question and answer were recorded on page 17, line 11. The question misstates "across the territory," and there was no mention of the Bijela Bridge. I believe this is a very important issue, and I think we should understand what exactly the general asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this will be short. I didn't want to do this, but because of the appeals judgement in the Dragomir Milosevic case, I have to put this question to you. Let me ask the Usher to put on the screen 3D44-0001, the first map we have in this document. Sir, we have this map on the screen. You see Mostar. Do you see Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I see hills on this map. Could you tell us whether there were any Serbian positions on these hills?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. All these hills that you can see, there were VRS forces there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're telling us, and this is now on the transcript, that the Serbian forces were positioned on the hills that we see on this picture. At the foot of this hill is Mostar; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this mean that the Serbian forces could fire with artillery on Mostar from these hills, either from Mostar east -- on East Mostar or on West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could open fire on any part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have no other questions. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. The Prosecution is ready. If we could just have a moment to distribute the binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meanwhile, Ms. Alaburic, in order to save time, we've just been told that next week's witness is sick and will not be able to appear. Therefore, there will be no hearing next week?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was informed yesterday that our witness is not feeling well and that he won't be able to come in, so I tried to contact some of our future witnesses, ones that were scheduled for January next year. But, unfortunately, yesterday I wasn't able to have somebody agree to come in on Thursday or Friday at such short notice. So for all intents and purposes, we'll be left without a witness next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is the last hearing for 2009, then. Ms. West, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My name is Kim West. I'm a lawyer with the Office of the Prosecution. I'm going to ask you questions this morning, and hopefully we'll finish today. And I'd like to start where we left off in regard to the area north of East Mostar, and in particular the roads that Mr. Praljak asked you about. I'm going to read to you some testimony from former witnesses, from Milan Gorjanc, who was the first Petkovic Defence witness. He was asked about this very issue, and I'm going to read to you what he said about the area north of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is from transcript page 46145. It's lines 5 through 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And he said --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but I'd just like us to bear in mind that Witness Gorjanc was an expert witness, not a fact witness, so he's really not somebody who, in the 1990s, was in the area himself. So please bear that in mind and how far his testimony is valuable with respect to the facts that we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I thank Ms. Alaburic for those comments, and I hope you will bear that in mind when you consider the IC list for Mr. Gorjanc because that's the very argument that the Prosecution makes as to why those exhibits should be excluded. But, nonetheless, the testimony of Mr. Gorjanc, in which he says: "To the north, where the main reserves of the BH Army were, there were two roads leading. One was down the Neretva River Valley, which was most probably under fire, under artillery fire, HVO artillery fire. The other route took one across a mountainous area, the western slopes of Mount Prenj, and on towards Jablanica, and that route was not under fire by the HVO."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in regard to his comments, he talks about two roads, the first being the road down the Neretva River Valley, would you agree with me that that's the M-17 through the valley?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: The main road -- the main asphalt road in Bosnia-Herzegovina is that road running through the Neretva River Valley and on to Jablanica. So the M-17 was used before the war, it was used during the war, and it's used today. So I see nothing contentious there. Now, were there any other parallel roads? Yes, there were several, not just one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to my question, which was: Is the Neretva River Valley the M-17? I understand your answer to be, Yes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so when you were answering questions from General Praljak in regard to the Bijelo Bay, and you saw a map, and you went around the map and then you went -- you continued on, is that the -- strike that. When you were speaking about the Bijelo Bay and you said that the bridge was out, and so you drew a line around the bay and then continued on, is that bridge and that main road, the Neretva River Valley road, the M-17?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see the M-17 clearly. There are two or three curves, but otherwise it's a straight road.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So I understand that your answer to that question is, Yes. Then would you agree with Mr. Gorjanc that the M-17, through most of this period of time, was under HVO artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but Witness Gorjanc never said anything of the kind. He was asked -- Gorjanc was asked for just one section of the road, and Witness Gorjanc clearly let it be known that it was questionable -- that his information was questionable as to what could be done and what couldn't. Witness Gorjanc said that theoretically you could target a certain region with the artillery, theoretically. He didn't say that something was under fire or not. And Witness Gorjanc doesn't know what the BH Army and HVO positions were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam West, in order to make sure that we don't have these useless objections, because we know exactly what was said by each and every one and we spent hours -- hundreds of hours, thousands of hours, pouring over the case; so in order to make sure that we don't run into objections, when you refer to someone's testimony, say, He said this on this page. And read the -- read what the witness said word by word. That way, there's no objection. And then put your question. But as you saw, systematically the Defence raises its it's feet whenever it sees a weakness in your questions, and we waste time. As Judges, we are here to control how the hearing is conducted. We have to make sure that no time is wasted. So my piece of advice is to quote word by word what the witness said. That way, we can no objection from the Defence. Otherwise, you know, if they object, it's an abuse of procedure, and then they would be sanctioned. So they won't object if you quote verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And as I said earlier, it's transcript page 46145, lines 5 through 10, and Mr. Gorjanc said: "To the north, where the main reserves of the BH Army were, there were two roads leading. One was down the Neretva River Valley, which was most probably under artillery fire, HVO artillery fire. The other route took one across a mountainous area, the western slopes of Mount Prenj and on towards Jablanica. That route was not under fire by the HVO." And that is the quote from Mr. Gorjanc.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, I now want to talk about the other route and one that you talked about as well. You spoke earlier about an access road after the Bradina [sic] Hill. You said there was an access road from Vrapcici which begins where Bradina [sic] stops. Do you remember that testimony 15 minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't think I mentioned Bradina. Bradina is between -- lies between Sarajevo and Konjic, and I wasn't up there ever during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, let me share with you some testimony from the Petkovic Defence's second witness. This is Witness Bozo Pavlovic, and speaking about this very same subject matter. This is transcript 46866 from November 16th, line 17 through 25, and this is a question from Judge Antonetti. And the question was: "You are saying that the M-17 was under fire or was exposed to fire. Very well. But was there another road that would not have been under HVO fire that could have been used?" And the witness's answer was: "I've just said, Your Honours, that I think that there was a road from the Zalik neighbourhood towards Vrapcici."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: "You confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "That's the other road." Mr. Peric, are you familiar with this road, a road from Zalik towards Vrapcici?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that. But you made a mistake. You said "Bradina," not "Gradina." Bradina is another hill towards Sarajevo. So there's Bradina and Gradina. And that is why I wasn't sure what you were asking. So it's Gradina with a "G" and not Bradina with a "B."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And the Gradina Hill that you spoke about earlier, is this hill located in the vicinity of this road from the Zalik neighbourhood towards Vrapcici?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so when you answered questions earlier from Mr. Praljak, it was this road that began in this neighbourhood that went to Vrapcici of which you were speaking; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I was speaking about -- well, answering General Praljak's questions whether there was a road from the shooting range downwards that you could communicate. So this was sheltered with -- by Gradina Hill. You couldn't see it because it was sheltered.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I would like you to look at this road, and I would like you to look at your binder. You have one right in front of you. If you can go to P11145, and this is a map. And I believe everyone will have it in colour. 11145, and this exhibit has two parts. There's both a map and then a second piece of paper with it as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Mr. Usher, if I can ask you to take the map out and take that second piece of paper so the witness can work with both pieces of paper. Thank you. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I think we all understand that you're very familiar with this area, so I'd like to tell you that this is a map of the Mostar area and north. And the light blue line beginning in the Zalik neighbourhood that Witness Pavlovic spoke about is depicted on this map. And he said that this road went from Zalik to Vrapcici and on to Jablanica, or this route did that. I'd like to ask you some questions about this. And for everyone -- to help everyone understand, and for you to understand as well, my questions are going to mirror the piece of paper that's located with this map, and we're going to start in Zalik. Would you agree with me, sir, that the first 500 metres of this route out of Zalik towards Vrapcici is a tarmac road and that a truck and a car could use that road?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I know what you're asking me, but I can't find my way on this map, where Zalik is and so on. It's too detailed for me to be able to find my way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Nonetheless, sir, you're familiar with the area, correct, from your own experience?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am familiar, but there are too many details on this map, it's too dense.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, then let's focus on my questions. In regard to this road out of Zalik towards Vrapcici, would you agree with me that the first 500 metres is a road -- a tarmac road that you can put a car on; a car can easily run on the first 500 metres?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But the second 500 metres, at least during the period of 1993, the tarmac road becomes a narrow path which you cannot put a car or a truck on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then the next 500 metres of that road becomes a very, very narrow path, and it's particularly along a cliff, which ropes were used to secure and support the users, and actually -- strike that. That ropes were used to help people climb up. So it would be the next 500 metres?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: As to that stretch, I can't say. But it's called a donkey track and -- or a horse track, and it's wide enough for a horse, bearing a load, to pass by. And there are paths and tracks like that all over the hills there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The next 18 kilometres of this road from Zalik to Vrapcici, now this -- you might be able to see this on the map. This is the road through Vrapcici. Do you see that along the light blue line?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And Kuli Livac? Excuse my pronunciation. That's the next village on that blue line?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's my village; I know it well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You were born there; correct? Okay. And as we continue up that blue line, we go through a number of more villages, Potoci, and it will continue on all the way to Lojpur. Now, this part of this road is 18 kilometres, and it's asphalted. And you can -- as you were saying earlier, you can use a truck on this part of the road, correct, or cars on this part of the road?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But once we get all the way up to Lojpur, L-o-j-p-u-r, and we can see this on the map, once we get there, going forward, the next 20 kilometres, would you agree with me, is a very difficult mountain path, and it's only accessible by foot; by fit, trained people; that the elderly and the maybe young children would have difficulty going on this particular 20 kilometres? Would you agree that's correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Have you ever been on this part?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: The village of Lojpuri that you're mentioning isn't there at all. It's in Bosnia somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you look, sir, at the map, and look on the blue line, and if you look at the area that says "Lojpur," can you find that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Lojpur is one thing, Lojpuri is another. They are two different villages, and Lojpuri is not in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if you go to the map and you look for the village that's spelled L-o-j-p-u-r - and I think you can find it; and if you can't, I can help you. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Lojpur [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I see that you're pointing to it right now. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You have to verbally say, Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At that point, going north on this light blue line, would you agree with me that the next -- the following 20 kilometres is a very difficult mountain path, would you agree with that, where no cars can go?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't agree that it's impassable over that length. A much shorter distance was impassable, as far as I remember. The other one was from the village of Glogova to Glogosnica, and that brings you to the asphalt road again, the other side. Now, I've never been that way myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Do I understand that you've never been on this path; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: From Glogova to Glogosnica, no. But from the village that you've mentioned, Lojpuri, is the village of Ravno, in fact, and Jasenjani, and I did go that way by car, a small car, a Golf-type car, but a bus could go that way, too, a big one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And when I asked you whether it was a very difficult path, you said that: "I don't agree that it's impassable over that length. A much shorter distance was impassable." So you would agree with me there is a distance that is impassable to cars, whether it be 20 kilometres or less?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I can agree only from Glogova to Glogosnica, that part of the road as being impassable for large -- to large vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Fine. Let's talk about Glogosnica, and that would be the next 2 kilometres. It's correct that is an asphalt road that cars can use; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: It's a road which took you from Jablanica to that place, Glogosnica, and that road is an asphalt road from Donja Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the interest of time, Witness, do you know what the jeep is, since you were a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. So my question will be very simple. Using a jeep, no matter what the state of the road may be, it was possible to go from Mostar to Jablanica? You see, that's all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until the conflict in 1993, it was possible. When the conflicts broke out with the BH Army on the 30th of June, 1993, for a period of time you could not go there in a jeep. You had to leave one vehicle and move into another vehicle and then continue on your journey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why was it not possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't possible because during that time they hadn't capacitated that road for car traffic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as I understood it, the whole way shown to us by Ms. West was a part that was under BH Army control. Wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was completely under their control, deep into their territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So completely under their control. Assume I am a BH Army soldier. I get on board a jeep in East Mostar. Can I go to Jablanica through -- using these roads or paths?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could go that way just for the first few months, and then you had to go a certain distance on foot and then get into another car, another vehicle. Now, when this road was joined up, then you didn't have to do that anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that the answer was translated properly on page 30, line 21. The witness said: "You could pass by on that road, but for the first few months..." And then the sentence continues. This way, it would appear that you could just pass through during the first few months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me return to my question, and listen carefully, please. The part of the road that was shown by Ms. West, was it under BH Army control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second question: I am a BH Army soldier. I get into a jeep in East Mostar. Can I, using the roads or paths controlled by the BH Army, get to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the first few months of the conflict, that is to say, from June, I think, until August, you couldn't go that way in the same jeep. Afterwards, you could, you could go that whole distance in one jeep without having to cross into something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why could I not drive the same jeep all the way through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there was a small section which was impassable to jeeps and larger vehicles, so you had to go a distance on foot and then continue in another vehicle on your way to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, sir, according to your testimony, there was a second section as well that was impassable to vehicles; correct? You had described it earlier. I said it was 20 kilometres, but you said it was less. So there was a second part that was impassable; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: The part that I know was the shortest segment, a kilometre and a half, up to two perhaps. I'm not positive about the length.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, look again at the map, and please look for the part that General Praljak spoke to you about, the Bijelo Bay. Do you see that on the map?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I can't see anything here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I approach the witness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, sir, now do you see the Bijelo Bay that you spoke to General Praljak about?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And through that bay, you see a black line. That represents the M-17 bridge, right, the Bijelo Bridge?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that there was a period of time where that bridge was down, and you could go around that area and still go north. But for the purposes of this map, would you agree with me, at least, that that black line going through that area is the M-17?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you circle the area of the Bijelo Bay, please?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you initial this map and date it, please, or sign it and date it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want an IC number?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, P11145, as marked by the witness, shall be given Exhibit IC01155. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to move on to a different subject. And you had spoken about the morning of May 9th when you were at the HVO headquarters, and you indicated that you heard shooting. And this is page 50 of the daily transcript, and I'm summarising: That you ran out to the -- in a hall, and there were two other duty officers there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that morning, you called Petkovic. You couldn't reach him in his car, so then you called Grude; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You also said, on page 51-52, that you telephoned the duty officer in the South-Eastern Command, and he told you that the ABiH had attacked; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on page 61, you said all three duty officers called, and I quote: "... all those people whom we were able to reach by phone." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And it's true that you said there was an unwritten rule that everyone should come in, and within an hour a number of people were coming in to the headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Peric, would you agree with me that that morning, on May 9th, there was definitely information flowing among people? There were a lot of people there, and you were all talking, and at least you and the two other duty officers were making several phone calls. Would that accurately describe the morning of May 9th?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: It's true I made some phone calls. It's true people came. They were probably woken up by the sounds of shooting, just as I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Nonetheless -- strike that. You also testified that you had no knowledge, and this is the term Ms. Alaburic used -- she said "evacuations." You had no knowledge of the evacuations going on. Is that your testimony, is sir?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you some testimony from another witness in this case. This is Zlatan Buljko, and this is transcript 19845, beginning on --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please, just a minute. Objection. As far as I remember, Witness Zlatan Buljko was supposed to be back for cross-examination, but then the OTP didn't call him. They dropped him. At this very minute, I can't find the transcript reference, but I will do my best if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, whether --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is entirely true. I would just like to join Ms. Tomanovic's objection, and I think all the other Defence teams agree.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter understood nothing because two speakers were talking at the same time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is true that he did not complete his testimony, the OTP has nevertheless a document, which is the statement that we have in front of us, that can be used to test the credibility of the witness. That's all. That's the rule. Do ask your question. Yes, Ms. Tomanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the Prosecutor is trying to use the transcript of a testimony -- of the testimony of that witness and not the statement. At least that's how they started out. If I'm wrong, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And, yes, this is the transcript, and this is 19845, and it's line 14 --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the OTP should not be allowed to use the transcript. They dropped that witness. The witness was never back for cross-examination. I will find the exact reference where the Prosecutor said that they were dropping this witness and that he would not be recalled for cross-examination. We cannot be allowed to use this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, the Defence for Bruno Stojic adopt the objection put forward in this matter. It is entirely inappropriate and highly prejudicial for the Prosecution to be allowed to cherry-pick evidence in this manner. They had the option of calling a witness, and the evidence could be heard in its entirety, not partial evidence, not the best bits of the evidence, but evidence that has been subjected to cross-examination. That has not been the case, and they must be estopped from relying upon untested, unchallenged evidence which they had the capacity of putting before the Bench in a proper manner that would allow Your Honours to assess it in its totality. Your Honours, for those reasons it is my respectful submission that the objection must be sustained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to discuss this matter on the Bench. I have my view, but I want to check it out with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After discussing the matter, the Trial Chamber is of the view that to the extent that the witness said in court certain things, even if they were not cross-examined, somebody under oath said something, made a statement. Therefore, the Prosecution is entitled to use such statements, but only in order to assess the credibility of the witness's statement. But the transcript, as such, is not going to be admitted. There it is. Ms. West, do ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. If I may just add. What I said on the record, I want that to be reflected. The transcript date is the 22nd of January, 2008. The page is 26463. The Prosecutor asserts that they were about to drop this witness altogether, just to make the record complete. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, very briefly just for the record, I do want it to be recorded that the Defence for Mr. Stojic expresses its disquiet about this development. It is not appropriate, in our respectful submission, for evidence to be assessed through the prism only of testimony of another witness. The proper form is for evidence to be tested by the individual Defence teams representing the individuals in the box. That has been denied us. We have been denied the material possibility to test that evidence. And to only look at -- or only to assess the evidence through the testimony of this witness is, perhaps, a partial, at best, and incomplete scrutiny to important evidence that the Prosecution seeks to get in through the back door now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: To avoid all misunderstanding, what Ms. West has the intention to do and what, in the view of the Chamber, it can do is put to test the credibility of this witness here today; but there can be, of course, no question of putting to test the statements that we have in the transcript of the untested witness, and the Chamber will definitely not regard what has been said by the other witness as an element of evidence. It will not be proof. It will either be not admitted at all or only for the purposes of challenging the credibility of the witness. And for that purpose, we have, according to our rules set down on the 22nd of November, and we have left open the use of practically any kind of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, so be it. The difficulty, of course, that will be for Your Honours to grapple with is: How is it possible to assess the credibility of this witness through the statement whose credibility you are unable to assess? It's putting the cart before the horse. You're seeking to establish -- or the Prosecution is seeking to establish the credibility of this witness through evidence whose credibility you cannot properly assess. That's the conundrum that the Defence -- that the Prosecution have to get 'round, and it's an issue that Your Honours have to grapple with at the end of the day. And it may be easier, in my respectful submission, simply to have asked the Prosecution to test the credibility of this witness through admissible evidence that has been tested or is capable of being tested, in fairness to the Defence. Your Honours, I'll say no more. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a single sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are wasting time, because I don't even know what Ms. West intends to ask. I don't even know what her question is going to be. So now we are having a discussion. It's intellectually very interesting, but from a legal point of view, from a judicial point of view, I don't even know what she's going to ask. It may be that her question is totally irrelevant, and this will have been a waste of time for nothing. Well, you will have enjoyed this discussion on credibility, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, since we are dealing with the Petkovic Defence witness, I would like to say two things, briefly. Firstly, if the testimony of a witness is never completed, if the Prosecution drops a witness, then that witness's testimony does not exist. A part of his testimony is not evidence. There is no document that we could call Zlatan Buljko's evidence. That's the first sentence. The other sentence is I'm just trying to rationalise and waste precious time. That is why I'm not asking for leave to appeal this. Nevertheless, we believe the Trial Chamber's ruling to be highly contentious, and we believe it would merit an appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, Ms. West. Put your question and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, this is from a witness who was living in Belanovica at the time, and he speaks about the night of 8 May. He said: "That night, on 8th of May, thousands of vehicles from Siroki Brijeg or Listica, as it used to be called, arrived in Mostar, and looking at all of this from my window, I wondered where all of those cars were going. And then there was a restaurant near my building, and I saw that soldiers were gathering together by that restaurant, and they were drinking, and I knew that something was going to happen." Mr. Peric, on the night of 8 May, you were at HVO headquarters; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were you aware of any soldiers or cars gathering in the city that evening?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you some testimony from Jovan Rakov, and this is from 24th of January, 2007, transcript page 12894, starting at 11. He said: "At about 5.00 a.m., some terrible shelling started. There was a lot of terrible fighting and shooting, and we thought, What's happening? Nobody told us anything. We switched the radio on. There were some proclamations which sort of said that an operation was underway by the HVO and the police forces, and that members of the BH Army were asked to surrender." And he indicates that he's paraphrasing: "Members of the BH Army were asked to surrender, to hand over their weapons, and to put white flags of surrender. And in the meantime, songs -- patriotic songs were being played. You could hear them. And then the wounded began coming in." On that morning, did you turn on the radio?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't need to. I heard none of the statements that you've been mentioning, nor, indeed, did I see anything that would have led me to switch on my radio or, indeed, turn on a TV set.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you see any white flags hanging out of windows?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your testimony, then, that on the night of May 8th and the morning of May 9th, you didn't see any of this, you didn't hear any of this. Would you agree with me, sir, that on that morning, being at HVO headquarters - you were in the center -- you were in the hub of activity for the HVO - would you agree with me that being there and being a specialist in communications, yet not seeing any of this, yet not hearing of this, is at odds with one another?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean? Did I hear anything about it on the radio? Is that what you're asking me about? What does this have to do with me being a communications expert? What could I possibly have used my communications expertise for? There was no equipment in that office. How on earth can you know what your investigators, for example, are doing somewhere on the ground, unless they actually call to let you know? There's no way you can know. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me. Mr. Peric, did you go outside? Did you look out the window?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: When the shooting began, is that when you mean, or do you mean during the previous night?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I mean on the morning of May 9th, did you actually go out and hear anything, and see any people moving around, and see any white flags coming out of windows? Did you see anything or hear anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I heard the sounds of shooting, and I tried to understand where the shooting was coming from. But I saw no sheets hanging from the windows. I saw no people moving about, apart from people running across the road between buildings every now and then on their way to work. I saw a colleague of mine run around and behind a building in which I was working, but there were no sheets hanging from any of the windows out there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, this might be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, I just want to clarify a couple things in regard to this path. Earlier, Judge Antonetti asked you a question, on page 31, line 11, and the question was: "I'm a BH Army soldier. I get into a jeep in East Mostar. Can I, using the roads or paths controlled by the BH Army, get to Jablanica?" And your answer was: "For the first few months of the conflict, that is to say, from June, I think, until August, you couldn't go that way in the same jeep. Afterwards, you could, you could go that whole distance in one jeep without having to cross in something else." My question, sir, is: When you were speaking about June and August, are you talking about 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then when you said until August, you could go that way, but afterward, you couldn't, what happened in August to change that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: That's when they had already broken through that part, making a macadamised road surface to link it up with the road going across the village of Ravni, Podgorani, across Livac, Vrapcici, Sutina, to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that -- I know that that part of the road was used. This was a section of the road that was broken through later, and they were better supplied with ammunition, they attempted attacks, and that was much better than from the 30th of June, or that month, roughly, until August.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the source of your information regarding that testimony is not because you were, yourself, were on that road after August of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it myself. I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at least from May of 1993 until the beginning of 1994, you, yourself, were never on this particular road that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: On the road where the bypass was made, no, I wasn't ever there during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to change subjects, sir, and we're going to talk about the details of May 9th. Now, you indicated that that morning, you attempted to make contact with General Petkovic, and you failed, and then ultimately he came into the office in the early afternoon; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And then in the early afternoon, somebody told you to try to find Pasalic on the phone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, was that -- did General Petkovic ask you, himself, or did someone else ask you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Someone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you failed in finding Pasalic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did Petkovic or anyone else ever tell you on that day to stop looking for him because they knew where he was?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: When we couldn't reach him, I told the chief that, and he probably passed it on further. So there was no more reason for somebody to tell me to stop calling him. Okay, you can't reach him. That's it, but I accomplished that task.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do I understand that it took you much of the day before you communicated that you could not find him?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, not much of the day. I needed half an hour for me to understand that through my own wire system of communication, I would not be able to reach him.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, on May 9th, you indicated that several -- many HVO people came in. You also indicated that on the ground floor is HVO Main Staff, but on the first floor is the Defence Department; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on May 9th, did you see Mr. Stojic in the building?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him, myself, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you know if he was there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What about Slobodan Bozic; did you see him?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I didn't see him either.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you know if he was there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you know who Vaso Vegar is?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat that, please? I didn't hear. I didn't understand what you asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you know who Veso Vegar is?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Veso Vegar, not Vaso. Vaso is someone else. Yes, I know who Veso Vegar is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: On that day, did you see him?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I saw him very rarely, generally speaking, while at the Main Staff, and I am not quite sure about that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You had, yesterday, spoken about the training and operations part of the HVO. Am I correct that ONO is the abbreviation for Training and Operations?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: ONO, an abbreviation, Department for Education and Training.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can go to -- back to Veso Vegar, you said you knew who he was. And did you understand that his job regarded public statements or media statements, that that was his role for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I know that he was -- we used to refer to them as "PD," representative, or chief, or that. But, yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And so he was the assistant head for information and propaganda; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now you have indicated that you came to the HVO Main Staff in October of 1992 and you were there at least until and through May of 1993. I'd like to show you a document, an HVO Main Staff document. It's 2D00687, and it's going to be in the binder in front of you. 2D00687. You'll have it on the screen in front of you. And this is a document signed by Petkovic on November 24th, 1992, so in a period of time when you were already with the Main Staff. Thank you. And I'm just going to read a portion of it. He indicates in it that: "In the past period, from the beginning of the war, there were individuals from HVO that issued statements to the media by doing which they revealed military secrets or in some other way diminished reputation of certain unit, headquarters, or HVO HZ-HB. "So that this wouldn't continue in the future, I command:" And under number 1 he writes: "Nobody from operational zone, headquarters, or formations can give statements to the media without my permission." Mr. Peric, would you agree with me that if anyone in the HVO was giving statements to the media, Petkovic was to be informed about it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Reading this order, that's how things should have been. Now, whether they actually were like that in practice, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's talk about the days preceding May 9th. Were you aware that Petkovic had met with Pasalic on May 4th for negotiations with SpaBat? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I knew in talking to my other colleagues. I didn't take part in any of that; I didn't see them leave or come in. But I heard that they had attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And let's talk about -- in those same days, about Bruno Stojic. Can you tell us, in the days preceding May 8th, where -- the whereabouts of Bruno Stojic? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you indicated that at least on May 8th, you understood that Petkovic went to -- Petkovic and Stojic went to the North-West Command for a tour; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I didn't conclude that; I found that written down in the duty log-book. I made no conclusion myself either way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, fair enough. So at 4.00 on May 8th, you looked at the duty log-book, and it indicated that Petkovic and Stojic were in the North-West Command, touring; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No. It said that the gentlemen you mentioned would be touring the Tomislavgrad Military District on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: On the 9th of May or on the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: The next day, the following day. So if I read "the 8th," it meant the next day two of them would be touring the Military District of Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction to the transcript. Line 4, when the witness said "if I read it on the 8th," this "8th" was put in inverted commas, as if he was quoting something.
