But he's not quoting anything; he's saying it referring to himself, "if I read this on the 8th," so without the inverted commas, because otherwise that could change the meaning. So just a normal sentence without the quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, I just want to make sure that we understand exactly what your testimony is, and I'm going to read to you a sentence from the summary of your testimony. You did not write this, but I just want to understand exactly where they were on the 8th and the 9th. The summary says that: "Peric knew that Petkovic had left Mostar a day before," so this would refer to the 8th, "together with the chief of the Defence Department, Bruno Stojic, to visit the Command of the North-West Operative Zone." Is it your testimony that you understood that Stojic and Petkovic were in the North-West Operative Zone on the 8th or on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I think I said that on the table I found a piece of paper on which it said that Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Stojic would, on the 9th of May, be touring the Military District of Tomislavgrad. And next to that it said that I could reach General Petkovic at such and such a number, that I could try and reach him on that number if something was needed. So that was common practice. They would always attach this to a page. So I didn't know that they had left on the 8th of May together, even less that they visited Tomislavgrad on the 8th -- the Military District of Tomislavgrad on the 8th. I didn't know where they were on the 9th of May, in the morning, either, as it said that they toured on the 8th. I don't know what it says on your piece of paper, but I said that they were supposed to go and tour the area on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that you had heard, or at least you knew from some source, that Petkovic had been with Pasalic at least on May 4th for SpaBat negotiations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard. Now, I don't know whether he was there or not. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So is it your last information -- or on the morning of May 9th, when you were making efforts to find Pasalic, is the last information you have as his whereabouts, is that information that he was with SpaBat?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I didn't have that information. Nobody told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, sir, is it your testimony that you didn't try to reach SpaBat that morning?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. We never tried; at least I didn't. And I didn't try that morning either.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're going to talk about the location of Mr. Pasalic that day, and I'm going to ask you some questions in regard to your ability to communicate regarding it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look at P1138 -- P11138, excuse me. And I think we have it up on the screen in front of us. And if we can go to the paragraph in English beginning at 6.1, but in the B/C/S it's actually 1.2. I don't know why they're different. So in B/C/S, it's paragraph 1.2; English, paragraph 6.1. So this is a SpaBat report -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise to my learned friend, but I would like to object to the way in which -- equally, in the same manner that Mr. Scott objected last week; namely, that is that there are no grounds to present this document, because the witness clearly said that he never communicated with SpaBat, nor did he have any knowledge of where Mr. Pasalic was on that particular day. So Mr. Scott objected in the same fashion last week, when the witness was asked about Sovici and Doljani, and Mr. Scott said at the time that the witness hadn't been there and so he doesn't know about that. So he objected in the same fashion that I'm objecting now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this document was under seal or not. Let me ask the Legal Officer to check this. Yes, obviously it was under seal, so it shouldn't be broadcast. Put your question, and we'll see much.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we go to the area under "Mostar," it says "Other information." "At 1850, a Spanish convoy escorting Brigadier Pasalic and Colonel Filipovic was detained at control point E5. At 2008, an officer of the HVO military police presented himself at the above-mentioned control point, reinforcing it and encouraging his men to adopt an aggressive attitude towards the Spanish convoy. Authorisation to continue was given at 2100 hours, but at 2140 the convoy was again detained at the Vrapcici check-point, where allegations were made of the existence of uncontrolled groups that are mining the roads. HVO sources have informed --" this is the captain of the SpaBat company, "... serving in the city of the possibility of HVO-BiH confrontations tonight." So, sir, let's first look at this check-point. It says that this convoy with Pasalic in it was stopped on May 8th, the night of May 8th, at 2140, and it stopped at the Vrapcici check-point. Sir, the Vrapcici check-point is within the South-East Command area; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, Vrapcici are in the area of the South-East Operations Zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So I'll take that your answer is, Yes. And my next question is: On the morning of May 9th, you actually called the South-East Operations Zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did they give you any information about this convoy being stopped the evening before containing Pasalic and Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No, nothing. They just said that a BH Army attack had been launched along the axis that I've already mentioned, and so I don't have to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's go to P02241, P02241. P02241. And in this, we're going to focus on paragraph 1.1. This is another SpaBat report, and this is the night of May 9th. It was written at 2130 that night. And under 1.1 for check-points, it says that: "On May 9th --" if the Chamber can indulge me, it looks like it says "10.00 a.m.," but the Spanish actually says "1.00 a.m.": "On May 9th, after painstaking consultations with Mr. Bozic, the Spanish patrol providing escort protection for Pasalic and Filipovic was allowed through the check-point at Vrapcici with the proviso that it must not enter Mostar and must make its way directly to Dracevo." Mr. Peric, can you tell me whether you remember Mr. Bozic calling the Main Staff during the either evening of May 8th or the morning of May 9th? Do you remember any phone call from Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And this information indicates that this convoy was allowed to go through Vrapcici, but with the proviso that it must not enter Mostar, and it had to make its way directly to Dracevo. Sir, would you agree with me that it was possible for the HVO to actually escort this SpaBat convoy through Mostar to ensure that it did not stop?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, they could have escorted it if -- from the positions of that check-point, crossed over to the side under the control of the HVO and passed through Mostar to Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. So you're suggesting that they actually didn't have to even go through ABiH territory; they could have gone through HVO territory to get to Dracevo?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that they could have gone through. Now, whether they went through that way, I don't know. Theoretically, they could have gone through that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And would you also agree with me that despite all your efforts to find Pasalic, at least at this point, after these painstaking consultations with Bozic, that at least Slobodan Bozic knew of his whereabouts at this time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to go to P02235, P02235.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the meantime while this document is trying to be found, just for the record -- I was trying not to take any valuable time of this honourable Court, but the entire subject matter, the questions which were put to the witness, is merely speculation. After the witness clearly said that he didn't contact the Spanish Battalion, that he didn't know about where was Bozic, then documents were produced, and everything is, Could that happen? He said, Well, I don't know, maybe, probably. Whatever, it is really speculation. So about 10 minutes, I guess, there is not any result -- any practical result for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, and if I can just comment on that as well. This witness was brought here to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just continue, just continue. You have eight ears listening to your questions and your answers, and I believe that what Mr. Kovacic just said was totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is a further description of the events at the check-point when SpaBat escort was stopped, and so this is 1830, 6.30 in the evening, on May 9th. And we're going to go to the part under "Other activities" in the English, it's the last page. I suspect it's the last page in the B/C/S. There, it says: "Transport and escort protection were provided for General Pasalic and General Filipovic from Jablanica to Mostar. The HVO refused this escort entry after a wait of more than seven hours. The persons escorted were taken to Dracevo where they spent the night and where they still remain." Mr. Peric, would you agree with me that in an event like this, where HVO units are detaining a SpaBat APC for seven hours, that in that event it would be very likely that the Main Staff would be notified of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a very serious objection. This is a topic now that was not covered during the examination-in-chief. I don't question that my learned friend, in conformity with the Rules and your guide-lines, should enter into a new area, but then she should know that leading questions are not allowed there. So I'm not challenging the fact that the Prosecutor can ask about UNPROFOR and Pasalic, but could you remind her that she must not put leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, in order for us not to waste time, let me remind you that the witness we have here was in charge of communications at the time. He does not know the documents that you are showing to him at the moment, but maybe you could cross with elements that he had in the Communication Centres with the content of this document. But please proceed wisely; otherwise, the Defence lawyers are going to rise to their feet and raise objections. Of course, we understand the problem. We're no fools. We see the documents, we listen, but you are working in a very technical fashion. But remember that this witness was a low-ranking officer at the time in charge of communications. He wasn't even the head of that department.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can I ask -- Mr. President, I absolutely agree. However, this particular witness, at 4.00 on May 8th, is the duty officer at the Main Staff. And as he's already testified, if things are happening out in the field, the information is coming to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then ask the question, what kind of information did he get at 4.00 p.m. It's interesting.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in regard to the information that I just read to you about this seven hours -- this check-point stop for seven hours, did you receive any information, during the evening of May 8th and the morning of May 9th, about such a stop?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I didn't receive any information at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You would agree with me that at least at this point during this stop, that somebody in the HVO knows exactly where Pasalic is located, although it was not you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't need to agree or disagree. If somebody knew, they probably knew, but I have no knowledge of anybody knowing. So I apologise to the Judge, but may I be allowed to expand and say something at this point? I came here as a witness for the Petkovic Defence. You had all my CV --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, that's not the problem. Ms. West is asking you, since you were on duty at 4.00 p.m. on the 8th of May, what information you received, because things are this way: Last week, it turned out that General Filipovic told us, under oath -- he took an oath, just like you did. He told us that he, together with Mr. Pasalic, were held. Well, I'm saying "held." They were arrested by the SpaBat. This is a major event. The number 1 BH Army man in Mostar was in the hands of SpaBat. And Mr. Filipovic, he was not just anybody. He, too, was held by SpaBat. That's what he said. And Ms. West wants to know whether you were aware of the information. That's as simple as that; that's all. The rest is secondary. I'm asking myself as well how it is that somebody who's on duty at the headquarters at the Main Staff was not informed of such an event, which, in my book, is a very major event. And the Prosecutor is trying to elicit from you whether you knew or not, so answer whether you did or not. Please continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know, but I said that already.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P02273, P02273. This is another SpaBat report, and this covers a period of time -- it's from May 9th, 1830, to May 10th, 1830. This is a report that covers 24 hours. It's P02273.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. West, are you sure that it is SpaBat, because here it reads "ECMM."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the part under Mostar says: "Access routes to the town are closed. Fighting has continued through the day. The HVO controls all access routes to the town." Mr. Peric, are you aware that from May 9th, 1830, to May 10th, 1830, that the HVO controlled all access to the town?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to continue on lower in the "Mostar" paragraph. It says: "General Pasalic, commander of the 4th Corps of the BH Army, is in the Spanish Detachment in Dracevo, and some HVO check-points have been put up around the detachment in order to prevent him from leaving. The deputy commander of the Capljina Brigade showed up in the detachment, demanding that General Pasalic be handed over, which the detachment commander refused. The situation remains tense, and the SpaBat has contacted General Petkovic in order to solve the problem created by the presence of General Pasalic in our detachment." So I want to go over this point by point with you, and it would suggest that during the 24-hour period from the 9th to the 10th, starting at 6.30, HVO check-points were put up around the Spanish -- SpaBat Detachment in order to prevent Pasalic from leaving. Is this information that the Main Staff received during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "The deputy commander of the Capljina Brigade showed up in the detachment, demanding that Pasalic be handed over, which the detachment commander refused." Now, considering your experience in the HVO, would an order to surround and arrest the commander of the 4th Corps be something that Petkovic would be apprised of?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: All I can tell you is my opinion, but it's difficult to say whether the information came through or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "The situation remains tense, and the SpaBat has contacted General Petkovic in order to solve the problem created by the presence of General Pasalic in our detachment." Mr. Peric, were you ever informed, on May 9th or May 10th, that the whereabouts of General Pasalic was at the SpaBat Detachment?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I received no information at all. Quite simply, even if such information had existed, which I'm not aware of, it would have had no way of reaching me. I have no idea why you're asking me to confirm all these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, sir, the reason I'm asking you is you were put on a task, which was to find General Pasalic on May 9th, and it appears from these documents, and I'll ask you whether you would agree with this, that the HVO knows exactly where General Pasalic is on the night of May 8th, the day of May 10th, the day of -- excuse me, the 8th, 9th, and 10th, that the HVO knows exactly where he is, yet you were asked to find him. Can you tell us, what is your opinion of that? Would you agree with me that those two facts, you were asked to find them, yet the HVO knows where he is, why were they inconsistent?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. Objection, Your Honour. The HVO had no way of knowing anything. Individuals within the HVO, perhaps. If my learned friend wishes to suggest that General Petkovic knew something, she should name him. The HVO comprised thousands of people. The question is, therefore, highly imprecise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecutor is saying that this SpaBat document, it is a written document that says that the deputy commander of the Capljina Brigade reported and demanded that General Pasalic be handed over. In other words, if this is an authentic document, there's at least one person -- at least one person within the HVO who knows that Pasalic is there, and that person is the deputy commander of the brigade. And there's also General Filipovic, because Filipovic is together with Pasalic. So there are at least two HVO members who know. And, by the way, last week -- well, I did not know that the Prosecutor was going to put these questions, but I have an overall view of the case, and I asked General Filipovic whether he was able to communicate during that time with somebody who was outside. I asked him whether he was able to, and he said he wasn't. And I, therefore, concluded that the information about this, quote/unquote, "detention" was not made outside, but here it seems that somebody in the HVO knew about it. So there's at least one person in the know. And you, did you know or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to go to P11139, P11139. You might be able to just get it right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is another SpaBat report, and this the next day. So this is another 24-hour report, and this is May 10th at 1830 hours to May 11th at 1830 hours. So it covers that 24-hour period. And we're going to go to page 6 of the English, which is the last paragraph of the "Mostar" section. So the last paragraph of the "Mostar" section. And it says: "General Petkovic --" Excuse me. We're going to go to -- it's not the last paragraph. My apologies. It's in the middle. It says: "General Pasalic, commander of the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, continues to be at the Spanish Detachment in Dracevo. The HVO has set up check-points around the Spanish Detachment to prevent him from leaving." So, Mr. Peric, this would tell us that this confinement continued on at least for another day, because this report spans to at least 1830 on May 11th. So now we're two days out after you were told to find Pasalic. My question to you is: Is there any information that you have at the HVO Main Staff as to the location of Mr. Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I'm saying this for the umpteenth time. I did not have the information. I didn't know where Pasalic was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Although you didn't know where Pasalic was, do you agree with me that it is clear from these documents that other people in the HVO knew exactly where Pasalic was, and those other people include General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, now I really object. This is a fact witness. How he is asked to conclude something? This is prerogative of the Chamber, not of the witness. This is maybe the question for expert, not for a factual witness, definitely. Even if he replies, it doesn't have any value. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is able to answer any question, and the Prosecutor asked a question and he answered. So, Colonel, did you understand the question put to you by the Prosecutor? Would you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what all these questions are meant for. I'm sure to answer "I don't know" in relation to each and every one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The purpose, well, that's known to the Prosecutor alone. But please continue, Prosecutor. But, Colonel, in this document we have in front of us -- look at me, please. There's a major event that took place on that day. At 1320, Lieutenant Arturo Munoz Castellanos was wounded, and he died later on. Was this a piece of information made known to you; namely, that a SpaBat officer had been wounded by gun-shot? Were you made aware of this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even such a relevant information was not known to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know that the gentleman was wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to P11146, P11146. This is an article. This is a newspaper article dated May 10th, so the day after the attack, and it's written by Veso Vegar. So on the B/C/S, you have the front page of the newspaper, and you have "Attack on Mostar" on the top, and then the article itself is actually on page 11. The front page of the paper says: "Attack on Mostar. Inserted groups of the Army of BiH Sunday morning attacked the HVO, Tihomir Misic Barracks. All the facilities have been defended. Seven members of the HVO died in the clashes. Mate Boban to Konjic Croats, 'Do not be afraid.'" And if we go to the actual article, it's an article written by Veso Vegar, and this May 10th, so published the day after you were looking for Pasalic. It says: "An attempt to take Mostar averted. Inserted groups of the Army of the BiH early Sunday morning attacked the HVO barracks. At the same time, snipers were heard in a number of the city's neighbourhoods, which the HVO Command interpreted as an attempt to take Mostar. All the facilities were defended. Two HVO members died and five were wounded in the clashes." And then the last sentence of the headline is: "Arif Pasalic on the run?" So if we go through the article, and I won't read the whole thing, but I would like to go to the fourth paragraph, starting with the fourth paragraph. It says: "The commander of the HVO South-East Herzegovina Operations Zone, Brigadier Miljenko Lasic, issued an order to the war hospital in Mostar to continue treating all the soldiers and civilians, irrespective of the unit they belonged to or their nationality. The HVO Operations Zone Command issued a statement calling all the members of the Army of BiH units currently staying in apartment buildings and other buildings in the town to surrender their weapons, guaranteeing them full security. Persons who are searching the apartments are warned not to take anything except military equipment and weapons." And it goes on to say that: "The statement indicates," and so this is at the HVO Operations Zone, Lasic, the South-East Command statement, "indicates that one of the main culprits of the current situation in Mostar is the Army of BiH 4th Corps Command, Arif Pasalic, who is trying to flee Mostar with the aid of UNPROFOR. According to the information available at the time, the statement was issued, the convoy with Pasalic in it had already passed the check-point at Zitomislic. The statement says that the attack on the HVO barracks synchronised with the activities of a large number of snipers, which marked a general attack on the town, was only a continuation of many days, long provocative activities of the Army of BiH, which failed to fulfill its obligation to abandon civilian facilities in the town. The Command of the South-East Herzegovina Operations Zone says that the aim of the attack is the taking of Mostar."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, this article was published May 10th, the next morning, after May 9th, and it would appear from looking at this article, would you agree, that at least Veso Vegar and the South-East Herzegovina Operations Zone, they appear to identify the location of Pasalic? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, excuse me. I have no choice but to object. That is quite different from the previous question. It's quite clear that Mr. Vegar doesn't even know where he is. He only hears here about Pasalic trying to escape from Mostar, which is very different from what the witness was told earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, sir, in reading this article, it talks about a statement issued by the South-East Herzegovina Operations Zone, a statement, I think we will agree, that had to have been issued on May 9th or very, very early in the morning on May 10th, indicating that at least Lasic knew the location of Pasalic; is that right? Do you agree with me that that's what it appears to say?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I cannot agree. I don't know. "Arif Pasalic trying to escape?" That's what I see here. It's a question, it's not a statement, an assertion.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. But we spoke earlier about media reports coming out of the HVO, and you had indicated -- I showed you a document about -- from Petkovic indicating that he wanted approval of all media reports. You would agree with me that if Veso Vegar is going to publish a story on May 10th, the morning after the events -- the major events in Mostar, that General Petkovic is going to know about this report; is that right, sir? Would Petkovic have known about this report?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. Mr. Veso Vegar appeared at this trial as a witness. He said clearly that he was the assistant of the representative of the Defence Department. He was in charge of IPD, and he explained to the Court, himself, how he wrote public communiques, how he communicated with the public, and that was his task. He had nothing to do with the Chief of the Main Staff or the Main Staff, itself, nor was he an employee of the Main Staff. Therefore, the order that Mr. Petkovic issued can in no way be in reference to the head -- or, rather, assistant head of the Defence Department, who later became the defence minister. I simply have to react, because my learned friend here is trying to link up two things that are totally unrelated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, here we have an article signed by Veso Vegar. In this article, as he puts it -- we don't know what information he has, but he says that Pasalic is together with the UNPROFOR. So how is it that he, an HVO member, knows this, whilst you, who were supposed to be on duty in the Communications Centre, you did not know where Pasalic was? That's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is simple, too. I didn't know because I received no information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, it's clear in here that Veso Vegar is suggesting to the readers that Pasalic has tried to flee Mostar. With that being said, would you agree with me that it's possible that Vegar fabricated this story in order to deplete the morale of the Muslims in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I can't agree. I don't know what he had in mind. I don't know what he thought he was going to achieve. "Arif Pasalic trying to escape?" He's asking himself whether that is, in fact, true or not. He's not asserting that Arif Pasalic is on the run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. You seem not to have looked at the document and listened to Ms. West and to the President carefully. You seem to be stuck with the headlines and the lead. But if you go down, you can read that: "... one of the main culprits for the current situation in Mostar is the Army of BiH 4th Corps's commander, Arif Pasalic, who is trying to flee Mostar with the aid of UNPROFOR." Full stop, no question mark. I am amazed that you always go back to the question mark part and do not answer the question on the basis of this passage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've never seen the article before. I had no time to read it. I'm being pelted with questions left, right, and center. It's very difficult for me to focus on a single thing. The kind lady reads something back to me. I have to check it. I have to see what it says. Nobody gave me this piece to read. And then I can read it and base my opinion on my own reading, and not on something that others are suggesting without me having seen the piece. That's the only way I can answer these questions. That is why I'm trying to be extra cautious. You know what they say, once burned, twice shy. Perhaps I should be allowed to read the piece myself, and then I can answer. Things being what they are, my answer remains the only logical one. I haven't seen this; hence, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, but you will agree with me that on the morning of the 9th, you did have communication with the South-East Command; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this article is based on a statement from the South-East Command, so is it your testimony today that in your talks with the South-East Command on May 9th, you didn't have any information that Mr. Pasalic was trapped in a convoy?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying. I received no information.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, is it reasonable to believe that the HVO purposely surrounded Pasalic, attempted to arrest him to ensure that he did not get to Mostar, so that it would make the HVO attack of Mostar easier? Is it reasonable to believe that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. General Petkovic wants to take the floor. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask you to ask the witness a technical question. The witness was on duty between the 8th and the 9th. On the morning of the 9th, he hands over and has nothing to do whatsoever anymore with any official information reaching the Main Staff. Ask him whether that's true. That morning, he handed over to a different person altogether, by which time he was not receiving any information from the operations zone or, indeed, anyone else. Can you just ask the witness that, and that will clarify the whole matter. Why does the witness not remember? Simply because he was no longer in touch with any sort of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it is important to know at what time you finished your duty shift, because we all were under the impression that you were still on duty on the 9th of May. And now General Petkovic says, No, you stopped your shift on the 10th of May. So tell us exactly at what time you finished and who relieved you, because otherwise it's a waste of time, because then you would no longer be on duty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been trying to say that for hours. I remained on duty until 7.00, or 8.00, actually, that morning. The general's secretary came along, and she took it from there. I was on my way back, as I said in no uncertain terms, to my office to go on performing the tasks that I was given on that day. I'm talking about the moment when the situation was more or less normal still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So he was no longer on duty at the Main Staff because the secretary had arrived, she arrived around 7.00 or 8.00, and he returned to his office. And so I confess that I'd forgotten about this so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, I'm going to ask you some questions about Mount Hum. You were asked by General Praljak earlier today some questions about it, and he, in the transcript, said: "You were in Mostar. After the two sides separated in Mostar, could you, from any of the HVO positions, see the Neretva banks controlled by the BiH Army from any point?" And you asked: "Do you mean Mostar or the broader region around Mostar." And he clarified, and he said: "Only that part of Mostar that was under the supervision and control of the BH Army, not what we can see from Hum Hill to the left and the right." And then you said you couldn't see the Neretva River or the embankment. So I want to talk to you about Mount Hum, and obviously you're familiar with it. The Trial Chamber has heard considerable evidence regarding it and much to do about the shelling of the old bridge, but I don't want to talk to you about that. I want to talk to you about it in a general, strategic way. Now, based on your experience as a military man and somebody who lived in this region, would you agree with me that Mount Hum is the highest point in the vicinity of the city?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: There are many higher points.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Nonetheless, would you agree from Hum a dominance of this city and the valley below it could be established, that it was an important military strategic point?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: In any case, it was an important defence point. Now, that it dominated the city, that that was that important, I'm not quite sure about that. Perhaps for the southern part of the town. But for the north and the other parts, it did not have any great value as a position.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You just clarified and you said that it was important for the defence of the city. But would you not agree with me that it would also be important for an attack on the city?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No, this -- for an attack on the city, it wasn't important in terms of domination. If I were to launch an attack on the city, I wouldn't rely on Hum. So it wasn't of major importance as a dominant point, having dominance over the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I think others would disagree with you in regard to that, but I'm -- and I'm going to show you a video, which is P06365. It's going to be on the -- it's going to be on the screen, P06365. And this is the Jeremy Bowen video. It's been admitted into evidence. This video was shot in September, and we're just focusing right now on an interview with General Pasalic. You can follow along. The interpreters will interpret. You also have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: September. Which year, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. September 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we just have a problem. I don't have sound. Does the Chamber have sound? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In your binder as well, there's a transcript of this interview with Pasalic, and I'm going to read that to you. He's being interviewed from -- by Jeremy Bowen. And Bowen says: "Away from the fiercest fighting, the Bosnian Army also controls the outlying villages to the north and south. General Pasalic, the regional commander, took us to see them. He's a professional soldier. He was an officer in the JNA, the old Yugoslav Army. Shells came in from the Croat side occasionally, but it was a quiet day and the Bosnian positions were secure." This is still Bowen speaking: "Even Mostar itself, five miles away, was fairly calm. The general, though, was not a happy man. He should have been in 30 hours of intense combat. His men battled their way --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, you didn't give a number of the document -- transcript in the binder, and I see that witness is trying to looking at the monitor where is something entirely else. So it will be confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The document number was given. It is P06365.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It may be well so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's on the record also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. Maybe I'm wrong, but it's obvious that the witness does not know that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It happens to all of us, Mr. Kovacic. I'm not immune.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, again, it's 06365, 06365. P06365. And this is the transcript of the video, and it's now actually on the screen. And perhaps the best way would be for me to slowly continue to read it, and we'll have the translations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could we have the page on the transcript, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. It's page 23, going in to page 24. And so I'll just -- I will read it again. Mr. Peric, I think maybe the best thing is for you to actually look at the screen. Okay. So we'll continue on where Bowen says: "Even Mostar itself, five miles away, was fairly calm. The general, though, was not a happy man. He should have been. In 30 years of intense combat, his men battled their way through a Croat-controlled suburb and up the mountain called Hum which dominates Mostar. It was probably their single most significant victory of the war ." And the next page, this is with Pasalic speaking, he says: "That mountain is the key. Whether you are attacking or defending, whoever wants to conquer Mostar must take control of the mountain, and whoever defends Mostar must keep control of the mountain because it dominates the city and the whole of the valley."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, now hearing Mr. Pasalic's full opinion on Mount Hum, can you tell me whether you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't think I could agree with everything that Mr. Pasalic said. But it becomes a little clearer, why he launched so many attacks on Hum with the object of gaining control of it. He needed to control it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would you agree -- would you also -- well, would you agree with me that in the beginning of May 1993, before May 9th and on May 9th and after May 9th, the HVO was in control of Mount Hum?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I can agree that it had the possibility of gaining that control. Now, whether they were up there at those positions, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to go to the testimony of Seid Smajkic. This is testimony in this case from May 24th, 2006, transcript 2536. It's line 4, and he says -- he's talking about May 9th. The question is: "Where were you on May 9th?" His answer, line 6: "I was in home, in my house on the right bank, right next to the demarcation line which was established at the time. In the early-morning hours, at dawn, there was fierce artillery fire, and attempts were made to expel the Muslim population and to expel people from their houses. People were expelled outside, they were in their pyjamas or nightgowns, and they were driven off in various directions. Since my house is located at the demarcation line, I saw right next to my house, with my very own eyes, thousands of people who have been expelled. They had been woken up, and they were expelled. They left in tears, with their children, and they passed by my house and headed east. And there was quite a large group that headed off in that direction. I'll never forget that event. There was crying, groaning, people were beside themselves. And while they were leaving, fire was opened on them from Hum and from other directions so that they would continue moving out." Mr. Peric, isn't it true that on May 9th, HVO had control of Mount Hum?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he did have control, but the possibility of gaining control existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I now want to talk to you about check-points and access to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to P02227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a follow-up question. I'm not going to ask for the video to be played again. But you were living in Mostar, at least you worked in Mostar, so I would like to know your opinion regarding an assessment made by this reporter, Jeremy Bowen. This is what he says: "Mostar is a city that is the most destroyed city in the former Yugoslavia. The situation in Mostar is worse than in Sarajevo or in Vukovar. This is a fierce battle, and it will continue for a long time." For those who might be interested, this is 35 minutes and 2 seconds into the tape. What's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that's a journalist professionally earning his money, writing to earn his money, writing things that the editor or editorial policy requires. To say that Mostar was worse than Sarajevo/Vukovar is absurd. Only a man who was well paid, had a high salary, could write anything like that, or for some other motive. But to say that Mostar was more destroyed than Sarajevo and Vukovar, as far as I'm concerned, that's absurd. I don't know. That's my opinion, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, have you looked at destructions in Sarajevo and Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the war, I saw the consequences of the destruction in Sarajevo. Now, during the war, I followed the situation on television and the images shown of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Vukovar, you've just blindly said that it was not -- that Mostar was not worse. But you have no real knowledge of that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't in Vukovar during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Afterwards, I went to Vukovar, but when everything had already finished, when the war had stopped. It might have been 1998 or 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you say you went to Vukovar in 1998. Could you compare the two cities, when it came to destruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You couldn't compare them. In Vukovar, mostly I saw destroyed small houses that were not from reinforced concrete, whereas in Mostar there's even a book called "Urbicide," I believe the title is, which shows photographs, and you can see what was destroyed and how much was destroyed. And I have given my opinion and said that the destruction of Mostar and the destruction of Vukovar cannot be compared, just as you can't compare the destruction of Sarajevo to that of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to look at P02227. This is an ABiH document from May 8th. 2227. It's only a two-page document. It's on May 8th, and it is to the president of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It talks about current events in Mostar. In the fifth paragraph down - I think you're going to have it on the screen in a moment. There you go. Fifth paragraph down, it says: "Mostar is being blocked on all sides by the HVO and HV forces, which do not allow Serb and Muslims to leave the town. Passenger traffic is interrupted, humanitarian convoys are being intercepted, and looting, and the drivers detained. The television service has discontinued for Muslims, although the television exchange is in working order." Mr. Peric, this is on May 8th. It reflects the events that day. Do you agree with me that Mostar was blocked in on all sides by the HVO and HV?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't agree with that observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Go to P02273. You looked at this document earlier, when we were talking about Pasalic. It's a SpaBat document, P02273. So I think you'll be familiar. It's page 3 of the English. It talks about Mostar. And I think if you look at the screen, you'll see it more quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, a quick question regarding the first document we saw. As far as you know, did the BH Army wire-tap the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the wire communication of the HVO or the radio relay system; which?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Land lines and radio systems, any communication system of the HVO. Were they eavesdropping on any communications systems of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everyone that has a device, including the BH Army. It costs 1- or 200 Deutchemarks or Euros, and they could listen in to the radio relay communications, which means that the BH Army did have that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking this because on May 8th Mr. Pasalic is writing to Mr. Izetbegovic and is taking stock of the situation in Mostar. If Mr. Pasalic had known that the HVO had a plan to attack on May 9, would he have mentioned this in this document? Could you give us your answer, as a military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had he known -- if he had known that the HVO would attack him, and on the 9th of May in the morning, well, of course, every commander would try and inform his superior about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And just to clarify as to who wrote this letter, it's signed by the 4th Corps Organ for IPD, Moral and Religious Issues, and then there's a signature on the B/C/S. Do you agree with me that that's not Mr. Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: This isn't Mr. Pasalic, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So, Mr. Peric, would you agree that if the HVO had blocked all access to Mostar on May 8th and that continued on, would it be fair to say that if the ABiH wanted to get supplies in on May 8th or May 9th, it would have been very difficult?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: From the south, from the southern approaches towards Metkovici, it would have been difficult; but towards Sarajevo, not. Well, it would be difficult, but not impossible. It would be difficult, but feasible, towards the north. Now, towards the east, the Army of Republika Srpska was already over there. So whether they used that access or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction to the transcript. Line 21, the word "Sarajevo" missing. The witness said "from the direction of Metkovici would be difficult and well nay impossible, but from Sarajevo it would be feasible. Did you mention Sarajevo, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] North, yes, that means from Sarajevo to Mostar. That was difficult, but not impossible. Feasible, I think that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, you've indicated that on the morning of May 9th, you called the South-East Command and received information from them that the ABiH had attacked certain HVO positions in Mostar. I'd like to talk about the issue of who attacked first, and I'd like to go to some of the internationals in the area to see what their opinion is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to P02241, 2241. This is another SpaBat document. We're going to go to page 3 in the English, under "Mostar." It's under the "Mostar" heading, and this is from May 9th. It's the evening of May 9th, 2130. And under "Shelling," it says: "At 500 hours, mortar attacks were launched against the Muslim sector from HVO positions." Mr. Usher, can I ask you to remain, because we'll have another one very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this indicates that it was SpaBat's position -- they wrote that at 5.00 that morning, mortar attacks were launched against the Muslim sector from HVO positions. Would you agree with me, sir, that at least SpaBat believed that the HVO started the attack on Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with that opinion, either with the SpaBat opinion or with your opinion. I have a completely different opinion, myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to look at the ECMM opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can we go to P02237, P02237.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is an ECMM report. It's dated May 9th. It says "Urgent" on top, and it starts with number 1, that: "The BiH Army informed us," being ECMM, "of the attack of Mostar early in the morning by the HVO units with Croatian forces. After checking by CC Grude, it is now confirmed that fighting using, in particular, mortars started this morning at 5.00 a.m., with clear HVO attacks on BiH positions inside of the town. Attacks were simultaneously conducted on BiH forces north of Mostar, halfway to Jablanica, in Dreznica, which is quite the last stronghold of BiH in the center of a completely HVO-controlled road to Jablanica. SpaBat has withdrawn from Mostar, where they had patrolled for three weeks. CC Grude tries to find new information without being able to enter Mostar itself." Sir, I want to focus first on this other attack. It says: "Attacks were simultaneously conducted on the BiH forces north of Mostar, halfway to Jablanica ..." Would you agree with me that simultaneous attacks in different areas, at a distance from each other, were likely not a result of coincidence?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't know that somebody attacked somebody in Dreznica. That's something that I'm hearing of for the first time today, and I don't know if it would have been the same as the events on the 9th of May in Mostar. I'm not calling them defence or attack, but the events. This is the first time that I hear that it happened at the same time at Dreznica, which is about 25 kilometres away from Mostar. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we can go to number 4 of this document. It's the last page of the English. It's under "Provisional Conclusion." Here, they're talking about the events on May 9th, ECMM is, and it says: "One cannot avoid that it is a new way to put pressure on the BiH Presidency just before the meeting of the BiH Parliament scheduled in Zenica for Monday with officially the Vance-Owen Plan at its agenda." Mr. Peric, you commented, in your direct testimony, about the Vance-Owen Plan, and I remember your testimony to be that in January, when the Vance-Owen Plan came out - and you understood that HVO signed on to it - you thought that the war would be over soon. So you're familiar with the Vance-Owen Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I know that there was one such plan, that a meeting was held, and that the representatives of the Croatian people agreed to the plan. And as soldiers, we were happy that the war would end soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But, in fact, that did not happen, and so at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: By May of 2009 [sic], you'll agree with me that that did not happen, and so by the beginning of May, only the HVO had signed on to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of May 2009, you say that the Vance-Owen Plan was signed; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If I did, my mistake. I meant 1993.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: You keep saying "2009," so I was wondering.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we be precise as to who signed, because different sides signed at different times in different months. So may we have more precision there?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, let me rephrase the question. In the beginning of May of 1993, the war was not over; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And there had been no agreement among any of the parties in regard to the Vance-Owen Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the Vance-Owen Plan was something that the HVO was in favour of; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, I have not seen a single proposal of the international community that was not backed by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness got the wrong interpretation. It might be a good idea for you to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter in the English booth did not understand the last part of counsel's sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so my question was: And the Vance-Owen Plan was something that the HVO was in favour of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. If I may be of assistance, I think the translation should be, the interpretation for the witness, that the Vance-Owen Plan was in favour of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, you're completely wrong. That's not what Ms. West asked. Ms. West asked whether the HVO was in favour of the plan, and the witness has actually answered this question in a way which gives the impression that he had correctly understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, please. Page 82, lines 24 and 25, the Prosecutor says: [In English] "And the Vance-Owen Plan was something that the HVO was in favour of?" [Interpretation] You're quite right. I do apologise. The previous question was different, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, you're going to move on to another topic. I don't think you have much time left. The Registrar is going to tell us. It might be time for a break, anyway. We're going to tell you how much time you have left so that you can organise yourself to make good use of the time left. Twenty-four minutes after the break. I hope there's not going to be any objection. Ms. Alaburic, I hope you'll have time for your redirect. Otherwise, the witness will have to return on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court's back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, before we broke, we were talking about the HVO being in favour of the Vance-Owen Plan. And my question to you, page 82, line 15, was: "And the Vance-Owen Plan was something that the HVO was in favour of; correct?" And your answer was: "Well, I have not seen a single proposal of the international community that was not backed by the Croats." So I will gather that your question -- your answer to that question was, Yes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we were looking at P02237. It's the ECMM document we were looking at before we stopped, and on the last page, number 4, under "Conclusions," it says: "One cannot avoid that it is a new way," speaking about the attacks on Mostar, "to put pressure on the BiH Presidency just before the meeting of the BiH Parliament scheduled in Zenica, for Monday, the following day, with officially the Vance-Owen Plan at its agenda." Mr. Peric, my question for you is: Would you agree with me that the HVO attack on Mostar on May 9th, the day before the BiH Parliament on May 10th was considering the Vance-Owen Plan, was a way to put pressure on the BiH Parliament to capitulate to the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] I think the facts are not being stated correctly, especially those that are already part of this case. Everyone knows that the Muslim side accepted the Vance-Owen Plan on the 25th of March, 1993. It's part of the evidence in this case. At the General Assembly meeting, which is also in evidence, the conclusion was adoption on a bilateral application to the Vance-Owen Plan. My only objection goes to the phrasing of the question. We can't ask something that is contrary to what is in evidence already in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when judicial notice has been taken, well, that's relative. Nothing prevents the Prosecutor from revisiting the issue, because she has no certainty as to the fact whether this Trial Chamber will draw the same conclusions from the judicially-noticed facts. And this idea put to the witness by the Prosecutor is an interesting one, and the witness is free to answer or not. Was there a similar -- a relation between the 9th of May and the session of the BiH Parliament on the next day? It may be so, it may not, and the witness may be able to shed some light on this. So you've heard the question, Witness. What do you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat? I've lost track while all of this was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West is going to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. West, the problem I have with your question is that it starts with an assumption; namely, that the HVO attacked the ABiH on 9th of May. This is an assumption that the witness has always denied today, unless I completely misunderstood, so I think it is not -- it doesn't make much sense. Ask him a question that is based on a hypothesis which he rejects from the outset.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for that point, and I'll take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So my question for you, Mr. Peric, is: Assuming -- assume, for the purposes of this question, that it was the HVO that attacked BiH positions and Mostar on May 9th, would you agree with me that the fact that the following day, on May 10th, the BiH Presidency was meeting to speak about Vance-Owen, that those two events, the HVO attack on May 9th and the meeting on May 10th, were somewhat related? And so, in other words, that an HVO attack on May 9th was designed to put pressure on the BiH Parliament at its May 10th meeting?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't think that makes any sense. If the Muslim side signed, why should now there be an attack being launched by us in order to jeopardise the signing of this agreement that suited us as well? Why would we try to make them change their minds about something that they had accepted previously?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, I'm going to talk to you about the military circumstances of that day. Now, we've spoken about three subject matters of military significance on May 9th, and the first is the control of Mount Hum; the second is control or access to the city of Mostar and check-points coming into Mostar on May 9th; and the third is the absence of Pasalic on May 9th. I want you to assume for me in this question that the documents that I showed you in regard to Pasalic's absence from May 9th are true. I want you to assume that to be a fact. I also want you to assume, because I know you disagreed, that HVO had control of Mount Hum on May 9th. And I also want you to assume that access to Mostar on May 9th was closed off to anyone other than the HVO. Would you agree with me that under those circumstances, that would be a less-than-ideal scenario for an ABiH attack on HVO?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I cannot agree. Let me try to speak hypothetically. The BH Army attack on HVO positions, it didn't mean a thing, that the HVO had control over the southern section of M-17, or, indeed, whether HVO controlled Hum. It didn't really matter. It might, in fact, lead us to the opposite conclusion. If the HVO knew that they had those points over there, that they were in control of that area, they probably would have thought that the BH Army would not be launching an attack. We could try to come to that conclusion, and, Let's try and launch an attack, so you're trying to do something against general expectations, and then you could put it that way. Why would the BH Army in that case not decide to attack? They might as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to talk to you -- we're going to move on from that, and I'd like to talk to you about the issue of Serb shelling. You spoke about this yesterday in both Ms. Alaburic's direct and also in the cross of Ms. Nozica. And from the transcript from yesterday, this is daily transcript 98, the question was: "Tell me, Mr. Peric, until ... 1993, was there this intensive shelling, and did the situation change later on?" And the answer you gave was: "The Army of Republika Srpska, is that what you mean? "Q. Yes. "A. Well, it went on intensively until about the end of June, and I think I described this and said that when one side ceased, the other side started. "Q. Are you referring to 1993? "A. Yes." Mr. Peric, we're going to talk about this a little bit more, and I'd like you to go to P04740. P04740. This is a presidential transcript, and obviously you were not there, but some comments were made and I'd like to know if they were consistent with your experience. This is the transcript from the 2nd of September, 1993, and we're going to go to page 10, page 10 of this transcript. And in it, President Tudjman is talking about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he's speaking specifically about the Croatian Army involvement there. And in the middle paragraph, he says: "In view of this situation, we have to suppress relations with Belgrade; that is, Serbia and Montenegro. I've already said it publicly, and I'm going to say it again, there is no ... nor has there ever been an agreement between Croats and Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding the division of Bosnia. It is a fact, though, that for five or six months now there has been no fighting between the Croats and Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina." So this is September of 1993, and he's saying "five or six months now," so this puts us before the beginning of the summer. Sir, would you agree with me that Serb shelling in Mostar really started to become sporadic and at a minimum beginning in 1993?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: The shelling occurred on a daily basis, but not at the same rate, hundreds of shells falling each and every day. Sometimes it was five shells, sometimes ten shells. So it could be defined as low-intensity shelling in relation to what was the case before. Nevertheless, it happened every day, and, it always came as a warning that there was someone behind your shoulder, Don't look around too much, just hurry up and walk along.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's talk about the shelling specifically in the month of May of 1993. And we'll go to P04740, P04740.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the transcript in English is not quite what I heard in French. It seems that you said -- I don't know whether there is a translation mistake. You said that there were five to ten shells falling every day, Serb shells. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said two, five, ten, maybe more. The shells were being fired from the positions held by the VRS. Were they Serb shells or Chinese shells, I don't know, but they certainly were being fired from positions held by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in principle, every day. Maybe they would stop for the Sunday mass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, we're going to talk about the month of May 1993. P04740. You'll have that document in front of you, and in a moment we're going to go to paragraph 26. This is a September 1993 UN report about the situation in Mostar. If we go to paragraph 26 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're making a mistake. I think it's not the right number.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me, I am making a mistake. P04822. My apologies, thank you. P04822, paragraph 26. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this is a September 1993 UN report about the situation in Mostar: "Since early May 1993, the east bank of Mostar is reported to have been subjected to constant shelling and sniping from HVO positions on the west bank of the city. Governmental sources claim that between 200 and 400 shells have impacted on average every day, destroying around 50 per cent of the buildings and 90 per cent of the private housing. They also allege that on 24 August 1993, HVO forces dropped mortar grenades on the east bank of the city from two crop-duster aeroplanes." Mr. Peric, it appears, at least from a UN perspective, since early May, that the east bank of Mostar has been primarily shelled by the HVO. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to go back again to this -- to the topic of this road going north out of Mostar. And I asked you some questions earlier about it, on page 23 of the transcript, and I just want to get some clarifications from you. So I'm going to read parts of the transcript to ask you to elaborate a bit. It's page 43. So my question was: "When you were speaking about June and August, were you talking about 1992 or 1993?" And you answered: "1993." And then my question was: "And then when you said until August that you could go that way, but afterwards you couldn't, what happened in August to change that?" Your answer was: "That's when they had already broken through that part, making a macadamised road surface to link it up with the road going across the village of Ravni, Podgorani, across Livac, Vrapcici, towards Mostar."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. West. I wonder whether there isn't a little mistake. Wasn't the first part that until August, you could not go, but later you could because of the breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Maybe I misspoke. I think -- so I'm reading from the transcript, and this is what I had asked: "And then when you said until August, you could go that way, but afterwards you couldn't?" And I asked him, What happened in August to change it? We can look at the transcript, Your Honour, to look at that, but my question is actually different.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, when you answered "that's when they had already broken through that part," my question for you now is: What did you mean by "that part"? What part are we talking about? What segment did you mean?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: That segment was the road behind Bijela Bridge that takes you to Jasenjani, and then it connected with a straight road to Bijelo Polje. Jasenjani-Ravni-Bijelo Polje, that road existed before the war. Another road that was there was the Bijela-Jasenjani road. There's a small section that went straight across the fields and meadows and some woodland, but then a new junction was made linking it up with the existing Bijelo Polje road. This is a textbook example of a bypass, if you know what I mean. The road was shifted in order to make sure that traffic continued smoothly. And I described for your benefit already what types of vehicles could be used on those roads and were, in fact, used.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I followed up with: "How do you know that?" And your answer was: "Well, I know that -- I know that part of the road was used. This was a section of the road that was broken through later." Again, can you clarify for us what section of the road was broken through later, and when is "later," when?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: The Jasenjani-Ravni section of the road was broken through. I'm not sure what time or what day. We are sure about that because suddenly a lot more weapons for the BH Army started pouring in, and the intensity of their firing increased. They were targeting us more and more. What this meant to us is that there was ammunition coming in, since there was a blockade further south. They could not have any weapons delivered to them, or ammunition, for that matter, from Metkovici to Mostar. They had to get it through Jablanica or else Bojic from positions held by the VRS. It was far likelier that they had broken through that section of the road, thus managing to get more supplies of ammunition from Jablanica. Knowing what amount of work was required to achieve anything like that, we were convinced, and this proved true after the war, that that was what they had, in fact, done. They achieved maximum possibility all the way from Jablanica to Mostar, without the need to change cars along the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. West, I'm sorry. First, the passage in the transcript is page 43, line 4, and I think it's -- my recollection was correct. But I wonder whether, if you want to continue on this "breakthrough" matter, whether it would not be very helpful if you could again show him the map that you had so that the witness can actually show where it is. I must confess I'm not quite clear by just listening to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, if you can go to P11145. It's the map that we looked at earlier.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I can't see any sort of map here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, why don't you turn in your binder and go to P11145. Oh, excuse me, I don't think you have it. I think we took it, so I'm going to give you mine for these purposes. So this is the map we looked at earlier, and you were just -- you were discussing the issue of the breakthrough. And I asked you what part of this area was broken through. Can you look at this map and take a pen and circle the section to which you were referring?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: This is a very small scale. It's very difficult to see that segment. Whatever I circle will be very rough. Can you just look where it says "Jasenjani," and then "Lojpuri," is not really a village; it's a hamlet belonging to Ravna village. You see, this is as far as the asphalt road goes from before the war, and then we have this little creek going towards Jasenjani over there. And then right next to it --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, let me interrupt you. You spoke before about a breakthrough. I want you to take a pen and show us on the map which area you said that they had broken through. Do your best.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks] That's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So can you put an A next to that, and can you tell us when it is that they broke through?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks] Sometime between July and late August, that's what I reckon. They had plenty of opportunities to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And so -- your -- the basis of your knowledge for this is not because you saw them do it, correct, it's because you suggest that they were then better supplied; is that correct? Is that the basis of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you then spoke about a section of the road that was broken through later, and can you tell us where that section of the road is? Look on the map and point it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, whilst that's being done, perhaps the map could be turned around so one isn't looking at it askance, as it were. It would be rather helpful to have it the right way on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, sir, now we're talking about a section of the road that was broken through later. I think for these purposes, in order to have the witness mark on it, it's going to have to face him. So if you could look at that map and mark on the section of the road that was broken through later.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: [Marks] I've marked it. It's here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So now you've clarified that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, to avoid any misunderstanding, because, as I see it, back in July and August 1993 the Muslim side restored this road and made it usable by car, so as of September 1993 you can drive on that road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Mr. Peric, to just make sure that we're all talking about the same thing, the road that you're talking about now, is this the road that you were talking about earlier that went around Bijelo Bay?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a correction to the interpretation. The interpretation we got was "Bijelo Polje," whereas the Prosecutor, in fact, said "Bijelo Bay." So just so that the witness is clear on what he's being asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We have a question pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, from what I understood, when he marked the letter A on the path, now, is the path in your map, because that's the map you produce, which is the blue line, and when we look at the caption, we see "back road;" do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that the -- when I asked him to put the A, it was just so later we know that that little mark he -- the black mark he put on the road is the A. I believe it doesn't -- it's not talking about the blue path. But perhaps he could clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for me it's the blue path. Witness, there seems to be some confusion. When you put -- when you drew this short black line with the A next to it, was that on the blue path? Did you put it on the blue path?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that I was asked to place an A on the section of the road that was later on broken through. Now, since it's too small on the map, I moved the letter A a bit. So that's what I understood I was asked to do, to mark the part of the road that, from July to August, was broken through. But I moved the A a little bit to the side so you could see the area, because it's all too dense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may also try to understand. This morning, Mr. Praljak asked you whether it was possible, coming from Mostar, reaching the place where the Bijela Bridge used to be but was not passable for a certain time, one could drive around this bay, north, and then back the other way.
