And you said, Yes. So that road apparently was available. Then Ms. West showed you the alternative road, which is blue. And at one point this alternative road does not quite reach, according to the map as I read it, does not quite reach the end of the bay. Now, does the breakthrough consist in making a link from the blue alternative road to the road that was pre-existent around the bay or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, now we've understood. Connecting the blue path to the road that existed until that time and which cut the journey from Jablanica. It was a short-cut and an easier road to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So, in fact, you agree that my interpretation is correct, that I have understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that you're the only one who's understood what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, that's at least one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so now that it's clear, then, just confirm to me: To go around the bay, to go around the Bijelo Bay, the black line leading into that is the M-17; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: The black line, yes, has gone into the bay, Bijela Bay. The M-17 passes -- it goes from the beginning of the bay, across the bridge, and it joins on to the M-17. It's a smaller, narrow road. It joins the M-17. And if you drive in that direction and turn right, you'll reach Jablanica without any problem. And you can't turn left, anyway, because that's where the bridge was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So let's just wrap this up. Say we're in Jablanica, we're at the top of this light blue line, and we come down and we go all the way to where you just put the black line about the breakthrough, and you take the short-cut and you break over and you go down alongside the bay, and then you get on the black line on the M-17 and you go south, Mr. Peric, will you agree with me, then, this route that you've been talking about going into Mostar is actually going by -- via the M-17?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I can't see how you're going to turn south from this road, from Bijela Bay, because you're moving in the direction of the north, towards Jablanica. Now, if you want -- if you're going to go towards Mostar, then it's the other way around. From Jablanica, then you go to the road at Bijela, you cut across Ravni, and you go down this blue road, road marked in light blue, although there are quite a lot of other ones, too. So if you know which road to take, you can get there faster, and that takes you to East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peric. I think that -- if you can just clarify this for us. In order to get to this breakthrough from the bay, from where the bridge used to be but then was not, you have to travel the M-17, do you not? You have to get on the M-17 to go up the bay. And if you're on the M-17, then you're susceptible to HVO firing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I want to intervene for a moment, because I've been noticing all day long -- I've been sitting here with my headset kind of off and listening to translation and listening to the courtroom at the same time. Throughout the day, throughout all morning, there has been audible comments coming from the other side. Mr. Praljak just did it now in a way that could be heard across the courtroom, and that is completely inappropriate. It has been going on all morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, no comments, please. Let Ms. West do her job, and let the witness answer. Continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. West, as it seems that I'm the one who understands: Witness, if you come from Jablanica, you can, of course, come on the M-17. Then you come to the place where the Bijela Bridge used to be, and you cannot go on, on the M-17. You turn left, and you go up along that small bay. And when you are all the way in the back of this bay, thanks to the new breakthrough you can now get on the road which is indicated in light blue and which takes you almost to Mostar, or towards Mostar, at any rate, in a way that is not the M-17, but is the alternative route. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, sir. I've been trying to say that all day. We're moving around that same route all day, but we don't seem to be -- well, I can't understand that she can't understand what I'm saying. If you're going to Jablanica, you'll reach the bridge at Bijela, which has been destroyed. She'll go left on this bypass and turn on to the light green line drawn in here, which represents one of those lines, and will reach East Mostar without having to switch cars, to transfer from one car to another. I've been saying that all day, and I don't seem to be making myself clear. But I don't see where the problem is. How can you not understand that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Correction, Witness. On line 20, you say "if you are going to Jablanica." What you meant is "if you are coming from Jablanica"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps it was the wrong interpretation. I'm sure I said "if you go from Jablanica." Maybe the interpretation was wrong. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, I think you've run out of time, I think. Mr. Registrar, could you tell us how much time is left? One minute, one minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Peric, just to wrap this up: If you're able to take that car all the way down the blue line into Zalik -- excuse me, to the Zalik neighbourhood and to East Mostar, when you earlier testified that the very beginning of this light blue line was impassable, how do you suspect somebody is going to get that car into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: When did I say that you couldn't take the light blue line to go to Mostar? Did I say that? I keep saying that you could use that road, that you could arrive taking that road. So tell me when you said you couldn't, or the interpretation's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, earlier today I showed you the aid to this map, and we spoke about the first 500 metres, and then we spoke about the next 500 metres, and then the next 500 metres, and then the next 18 kilometres. Don't you remember indicating that there was a 500-metre section that was not passable for cars?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I did say that, yes. That doesn't mean that they used that section. They used the M-17, because on the other side of the Neretva River there's the village of Rastani also controlled by the BH Army, so I see no reason why someone would take the mountain route if the M-17 was open and under their control. Now, you keep referring to a couple of kilometres up there. All I said was that there was the possibility for that, there was that option.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: But whether they used it, no, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Peric. But would you agree with me that the M-17 was so close to the HVO confrontation line that it was susceptible to HVO fire?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No, there wasn't that danger, and it didn't happen. Not a single BH Army soldier was killed by an HVO bullet.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour, but I hope to get through them quickly, relatively quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us, Witness, that no HVO Army soldier was killed because he used the road north of Mostar in the direction of Jablanica. Tell us whether any civilians were killed, perhaps, because they might have been on one of those roads north of Mostar, in the direction of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, the document with an A, do you need an IC number for it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This second marked version of document P11145 shall be given Exhibit IC01156. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, let me ask you again. Did it ever happen that a civilian was killed on any of the roads running from Mostar in the direction of Jablanica, to the north?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I don't know that that ever happened, but I do know that a -- one of our captured soldiers were killed by the BH Army, and he was taken from Mostar to Bijelo Polje every day for trench-digging. That we do know, and you can read about it in the reports, the reports about those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago, Witness, when speaking about breaking through at Jasenjani, the road there, you said that you knew that the road had been broken through because the BH Army had greater quantities of ammunition, you felt that there was more intensive fire on the part of the BH Army, hence more ammunition, and then you said that after the war you, yourself, saw these newly-built roads. When you were asked again by the Prosecutor as the source of your knowledge about the breaking through of this road, the answer was suggested that you must know that because of the information you received about greater quantities of ammunition that reached the BH Army, and that is why I would like to ask you the following: When the conflict ended with the BH Army, did you establish or learn that that section of the road through that way to Jablanica was actually broken through? Did you see that, yourself?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: A lot of the things I'm saying, I'm saying because I learnt later on in talking to people who were my adversaries until yesterday, my neighbours, but we still talk normally to each other. We haven't severed our communications, our links. And they told me the soldiers from the BH Army who had switched sides from the HVO and gone to join the BH Army, they told me about that. But I was asked how I knew then that the road was broken through. We assumed that it had been broken through because they knew the lay of the land and that it didn't represent a great problem. You only needed a dredger and could break through that way. And we concluded they had actually done that, succeeded in doing that, judging by the intensity of the firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. And later on, all this was confirmed by your colleagues who were Muslims; is that right? Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, you have. After the war, I say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Now let's try, briefly, to clear up some of the loose ends, some of the details. Towards the end of your examination, when Judge Antonetti, I think, asked a question -- no, it was at General Petkovic's intervention, when it was cleared up that duty shifts lasted until about 8.00 a.m., I'd like to remind everybody that yesterday the witness spoke about this and it was recorded on page 18 of the transcript, and there was no doubt at all that shifts lasted until 8.00 a.m. So tell us now, please, Witness, at the beginning of our discussion yesterday, did you consider that you clarified this point, that your duty shift ended at 8.00 a.m. and that there was no need to say that on that day, the 9th of May, 1993, you were no longer the duty officer because your shift was over?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, I was very explicit on that point, and now I'm wondering, myself -- asking myself the question of why I'm speaking if nobody is listening to me, if nobody wants to hear me. You shouldn't have brought me in here in the first place. Everything that I've said has -- attempts have been made to turn it around. I have come here to help the honourable Trial Chamber and to help the person that called me as a Defence witness, but I seem to have placed myself at the disposal of the Prosecution for them to ask me what I know about, what -- there's no point in me telling you what other people told me, because you could reach those people directly and have them tell you. But when I give an opinion, I don't see you asking me what my opinion is for me to be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, there's been a lot of information, and please rest assured that all of us in this courtroom are trying our best -- are doing our best to understand you, and that's why we are clarifying certain points. Now, tell me, when General Petkovic arrived at the Main Staff in the early hours of the afternoon of the 9th of May, 1993, you told us that you received a request telling you to try and establish contact with Mr. Pasalic, and you also told us that that request you did not get directly from General Petkovic, but that it was conveyed to you by a certain individuals. So please tell us now the first and last name of that particular individual.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: It's my chief for communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Jure Zadro. Do you need more explanation as to why that happened, how it came about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to disturb you during the very last minutes, but I would like to note that Mr. Peric has stated a few minutes ago that, There is no point in me telling you, et cetera, about the problems, because nobody is listening to me. I believe that I have to point out that it is not a correct way of putting your opinion here. You cannot know who is listening to you and who is not, in the first place. And, secondly, no doubt that there are a great number of people here who are interested in listening to your explanation and positions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Prandler. I think that the witness realises that, but he probably didn't use the right words to express himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Peric, could you briefly explain to us why Jure Zadro conveyed this request, telling you to call Arif Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Because he was the chief of the Communications Department; my immediate superior, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was the person from your subsection who mostly communicated with General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: It was the chief of the department.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Zadro; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Peric, you were asked about UNPROFOR vehicles moving from Jablanica towards the south, and in one of these vehicles there was Arif Pasalic inside. Now, you were shown documents, and you were told that the vehicles were stopped at a check-point at Vrapcici. My question to you now is this: If you are travelling from Jablanica in the direction of Mostar, and you're stopped at Vrapcici, and you wish to continue your journey south, do you have to pass through East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, you do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, East Mostar, that night, between the 8th and 9th of May, 1993, was it under the control of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Now, Mr. Peric, do you happen to know that the BH Army -- whether the BH Army or any of its commanders at any point in time wrote reports, mediated, informed people as to whether Arif Pasalic was in Dracevo and that he couldn't return from Dracevo to Mostar, and all because of the HVO's conduct? Did you ever hear of anything like that happening?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Peric, in response to a question about the destruction of Mostar, you compared Mostar to Vukovar and Sarajevo. It is a thankless task to compare towns and cities that have been destroyed in a war, but His Honour Judge Trechsel asked you how come you know how Vukovar and Sarajevo were destroyed, the degree of destruction there. So I'm going to ask you whether you ever saw footage of or pictures of Vukovar destroyed, the destruction in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And did you also see footage of the destruction of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Certainly more times than I saw Vukovar being destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, my learned colleague Ms. West showed you a document, and you can just listen to me - you needn't look at it - P4822. 4822, that's right, and it's a report -- a UN report about the events in Mostar in May 1993, and there was mention of HVO attacks -- alleged attacks on Eastern Mostar, then 200 to 400 shells falling, and so on and so forth. Now, I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph 26 of this document, which was used and presented to you. Now, the person who compiled this report says this is information from government sources, obtained from government sources. Now, tell us, if an international observer defines its local sources in that way, does that mean the government in Sarajevo or the Muslim side in the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever you say "government sources," it means Sarajevo, because they saw Sarajevo as the capital, the main city, and hence the government in Sarajevo. So that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what Mostar looked like after the war with the Serbs in Mostar, and then also how the Serb artillery continued to pound Mostar? Do you know what Mostar ended up looking like because of the pounding by the Serb artillery?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I crossed Mostar quite a number of times at the time. There are many photographs and quite a lot of footage showing the extent of destruction. We may as well say that it was the same amount of destruction as in 1995, and you can tell that if you look at the footage. Was there any further destruction that was wreaked when the BH Army and the HVO shelled each other? Yes, there was some more, but in no way particularly striking. The old part of Mostar, the east part of Mostar, was destroyed on the 19th of June, 1992. When I first arrived, it was destroyed already, the 19th or the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, the Prosecutor asked you about the clashes in Mostar on the 5th of May. She put to you the following theory: The Croats accepted the Vance-Owen Plan. There was a BH Assembly meeting scheduled for the 10th of May, where they were supposed to take a decision regarding the acceptance of the Vance-Owen Plan by the Muslims, as one of the warring sides. The Croats then launched an attack in Mostar in order to exert more pressure on the Muslim side to accept the agreement. Do you remember that hypothesis that was put to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, you answered it would have been illogical for the Croats or anyone else to jeopardise a plan that they had already agreed to. Can you please comment on the following hypothetical situation or theory which I'm about to put to you: The BH Assembly is scheduled to take place on the 10th of May, 1992. There are certain factions within Bosnia and Herzegovina that are not on the same frequency as Alija Izetbegovic, who in late March 1993 had signed the Vance-Owen Plan. For this reason, they are trying to bring about fierce clashes with the Croats in order to show to everyone how impossible it was to co-operate with the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. How about this kind of scenario, sir? Does that look plausible to you? Does it look likely or possible?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: If you really want my opinion, yes, I think that is a distinct likelihood.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My last topic. We won't be dealing with the roads, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speed up, do speed up, because we are already going towards 15 minutes over time now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I'll take no more than two or three minutes. The documents that the Trial Chamber has seen or -- just listen to me, Mr. Peric. The first document is 4D719, which is a report of the 4th Corps of the BH Army. Among other things, it talks about communications in and around Mostar. It reads: "A huge problem for the command of the operations group is posed by the transport of civilian population and everyone else marching north and south. It is, therefore, necessary for the civilian authorities to take charge of the transport of civilians."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge, Mr. Peric, were the civilians physically able to leave East Mostar if they so desired?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would have been able to leave and head on to Sarajevo at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The report goes on to state: "The problems are huge regarding transport of the wounded and everyone else into the town of Mostar." It also talks about how necessary it is to fix an APC to be used at night-time. Witness, based on your information, and based on such statements as were used during your examination-in-chief, do you know anything about the fact that the wounded were brought in to the Mostar hospital or, indeed, that prisoners, for example, were taken to perform labour anywhere outside East Mostar? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just another detail from this document: It says that firewood for bakeries is being brought into Mostar on a daily basis, and then the bread is taken out of Mostar towards Bijelo Polje. What about the communication between Bijelo Polje and Mostar? According to you, what you knew about that, did it go on operating smoothly all this time following June 30th, 1993, which we believe to be of a [indiscernible] intention?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was operating like that. It reads that bread was being driven out of Mostar, not carried. I think that shows what you're trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it's precisely along this segment on the way into East Mostar in relation to which Ms. West put it to you that one could only walk, but not drive?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The last document and my last question: 4D545. This is an excerpt from Esad Sejtanic's book, "Herzegovinians at the Fiery Gate of Bosnia." Let's see what the Muslim commanders, themselves, say about this particular line of communication: "The situation in Mostar, itself, and around was becoming more and more difficult. Famine was rife. The little food that got into Mostar from Jablanica and Glogova was being distributed in meager rations. A large number of the inhabitants still wanted to leave and go to Jablanica and then further into Bosnia. Unfortunately, we had to take repressive measures to prevent the population from leaving and to reduce all movements to a bare minimum." Mr. Peric, did you ever hear anything to the effect that the military commanders of the BH Army were keeping civilians from East Mostar from leaving Mostar if they so desired?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my cross-examination. Thank you very much, Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your testimony has now come to an end, Colonel. I want to thank you for coming to The Hague to testify, on behalf of my fellow Judges. Sometimes you have the impression -- have had the impression that you were misunderstood, but I can assure you that you were listened to at all times. So I thank you for your testimony, and I'll ask the Usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just address the Court very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry, it can't be done. Mr. Kovacic, you have two minutes. You wanted to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It's really difficult for me to ask for another two minutes at the close of business, but we have no choice. On the 30th of November, 2009, this Trial Chamber was kind enough to allow us to reply to the five responses filed by the other parties in this case, their responses to a documentary motion. You ruled in our favour and gave us a dead-line, which was the 14th of December. We are still trying to abide by that dead-line. Nevertheless, we have been facing certain problems in the meantime. The problems, themselves, would not have kept us from abiding by the dead-line, but as you know, the Prosecution has lodged an appeal in relation to the provisional release of General Praljak. Now we are facing a huge dilemma: How do we prioritise? One priority would be we have to respond to that appeal as quickly as possible to keep things running smoothly. The other priority was the dead-line that we were given. We would like to please ask the Trial Chamber to give us another two days and change the 14th to the 16th, to set a new dead-line for two days later. I don't think there's any prejudice to the other party, and I don't think the Chamber will be ruling the very next day. That is my request and my motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After discussing the matter, the Trial Chamber is granting you two additional days. So the dead-line is now 16th of December for filing your submissions. As you know, this is going to be our last hearing day in 2009. We shall reconvene in January, so let me use this opportunity to wish you all a very happy festive season and to gather forces for the months to come, because we'll be in the last leg of this trial by then. So this was my wish to all of you. I think we'll resume on Tuesday [as interpreted], the 11th of January, at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of January, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.02 p.m.,
